- - The Old-Time Printers' Association of Chicaao gave a banquet on the evening of January rith, in honour of Ben Franklin. Among those present Mrs. 1. M. Burger recited, in an effective and pleasing manner the following "poem" entitled--

THE PRINTER'S TOWEL. When [think of the towel, the old-fashioned towel, I That used to hang up by the printing-house door, I think that nobody, in these days of shoddy, Can hammer out iron to wear as it wore. The tramp who abused it, the devil who used it, The comp. who got at it when those two were gone, Ape make-up and foreman, the editor, poor man, Each rubbed some grime off while they put a heap on. In, over, and under, it was blacker than thunder, Harder than poverty, rougher than sin; From the roller suspended it never was bended, And it flapped on the wall like a banner of tin. It grew thicker and rougher, and harderandtougher, And daily put on a more inkier hue; Until one windy morning, without any warning, It fell to the floor and was broken in two.

The oldest settler in the West—The sun. We always imagine what has not happened the best. Innocence is like polished armour; it aderns and it ,defends. It is easier to suppress the first desire than to satisfy all that follow it. No cat has two tails. A cat has one tail more than no .cat. Ergo—A cat has three tails. Better be good than greats You'll have less competi- tion. The latter business is overdone. - Women rarely are great inventors, though 'they are often the first to discover new wrinkles. There's nothing like leather, exeepting„ of course, the upper crust of the young wife's first pie. We are strange instruments. We never know what 'tune the touch of the next moment will play. The greatest trial of patience is a stammering barrister examining a stuttering witness in the presence of a deaf judge. "That motion is out of order," said the chairman of a political meeting, as he saw a rowdy raising his arm to throw an egg. The bravest is he who does not hesitate before danger —the most upright is he who does not .hesitate to do. that which is right. We pleasantly weave beauty out of beauty, good out of goodness. instead of striving to develop ugliness into beauty and evil into rood. "It is a solemn thing to be married," said Aunt Rachel, a grave spinster, to her niece. "It's a good deal more solemn not to be," said the merry. girl. A Western paper kindly supplies this beautiful simile. "You might as well try to shampoo an elephant with a thimbleful of soapsuds as attempt to do business and ignore advertising. Two gentlemen calling at the house of one who bore the name of Fish, and observing the portraits of the children of the family on the walls, one of them remarked to his companion," Sardines." "Yes," replied the other, "Little fishes done in oil." Be: "They are in great trouble here at Dawson's, you know." She.: They are?" What about?" Be: "Why, Dawson's chef ran Off with his daughter this morning, and Dawson had invited half the town to a big dinner to-night. Dawson says he'll discharge him if he is his son-in-law ten times over." "What do you wish ? " asked the servant who answered a ring at the door. "Baron de Veauminet." "What do you wish to see him for?" "It is in relation to a promissory note." "The Baron went out of town yesterday." That is too bad; I wanted to pay him the amount I owe him." "But," added the servant, "he returned this morning." The Khalif, Aleaschid, was accosted one day by a poor woman, who complained that his soldiers had pillaged her house and laid waste her grounds. The Khalif de- sired her to remember the words of the Alcoran, "That when princes go forth to battle the people through whose fields they pass must suffer." "Yes," says the woman. "but it is also written in the same book that the habitations of those princes who authorise the in- justice shall be made desolate." This bold and just reply had a powerful effect on the Khalif, who ordered imniediate reparation to be made. A small boy was one day calling on a school friend, and fell into conversation with his friend's mother. Be finally remarked that it was getting very hard to tell, from the places in which people live, whether or not they are entitled to social consideration. "Now there's Blank-street," he said, "you wouldn't think anybody was much that livea in Blank-street, would you? But there's Mr. T—, he lives there." "And is Mr. T— ' much?" "Mr. T—?" with astonishment. "I should think he was ! He's an awful swell. Why, he won't speak to my father!" A DESIRABLE Mornee-ne-Law.—A great many stories have been told about men who had no use for their mothers-in-law; hence an exception to the general rule is very refreshing. "I don't want to hear Or read any- thihe disparaging to mothers-helaw," said Judge Peter- by to his young friend Hestetter M‘Ginnis. "What makes you talk in that eccentric sort of way, judge?" "I'll tell you why. My wife has jawed me almost to death ever since we were married. Last week,' invited her mother to come over from St-Louis and live with us." "Mien alive, have you lost your senses ?" "Not much. You see they don't agree. They fight each other all day long, and I'm enjoying a season of heavenly rest. My wife is so tired quarrelling all day long with her mother, that when I come home there is nothing lett over for me. Why, that mother-in-law of mine is a lightnine rod. I feel perfectly safe as long as she is in the house. She is a treasure. The next man I hear abusing mothers-in-law has got me to fight. I only wish I had three or four of them in my house, then I'd feel perfectly safe."—American Paper. THE RAT AND THE TELEGRAPH WIRE.—As most people know, remarks a writer in the Cornhill, the main tele- graph wires in London run through the subways in which the gas-pipes and sewers are placed. The princi- pal arteries are so large that it is easy enough for men to work in them, but the pipes through which the side. wires branch off are much smaller, and great care has to be taken to preserve the connection between the main and lateral wires. Some years ago men were repairing one of these latter, and carelessly omitted to attach it to a leading-line by which it could be drawn to its place when mended. The blunder seemed likely to have seri- ous consequences, for it was thought that the whole of the lateral pipe would have to be dug up in order to get at the broken wire. But one of the men came to the rescue with a happy thought. suggesting that a rat should be procured, and with a fine piece of wire attached to it, sent through the pipe. This was done; but, to the dismay of the workmen, the new hand came to a stop after it had gone a few yards. The inventor of this idea was not yet, however, at the end of his resources, and by his advice a ferret was procured and started on the dilatory rani track. There was a moment of suspense before it was settled whether the rat would show fight or run away, but this was soon ended by the paying-out of the wire, and in a short time the latest addition tcr the staff of the Post Office appeared at the other end of the pipe. It was caught, the wire detached, and then it was set free in recognition of the service it had rendered. By means of the wire the telegraph line was secured, and a long and laborious piece of work saved. Ha Foaocer THE RABY.—The prize absent-minded man of the century is a well-known railroad official living in Chicago. He is a young man, but he some- times really forgets that he is living. Just now there is a pretty little baby up at his house—a now arrival—and now he IS more absent-minded than ever. He is obliged to look after domes& affairs since his wife's illness, and he is not used to the task. He knows all about differ- ential rates, but he cannot tell a stove from an ice-chest. The other morning he arose and built a fire in the kitchen stove. When he closed the oven door he forgot all about the pet kitten who seeks the oven as a nightly resting place, and when the oven was opened later on the pet kitten was found, done to a turn. The roasting which the young man received over this was quite as bad. But he does like the new baby, and he embraces every opportunity to embrece it. The other morning he begged it from the nurse and took the youngster into the library. Sitting before his big desk he rattled the pens and paper-weights for the baby's amusement until there came a sharp ring at the front door bell. Hastily laying the baby upon the desk he slammed dewn the desk curtain and rushed to the door. It was a friend who wanted to see him on business, and he put on his hat and coat and walked out with him, forgetting all about the baby in the desk. When the nurse came to take it she could not find it. The young man's hat and coat were gone, and she feared he had taken the baby out into the cold with him. The house was in a tumult. When he returned, half an hour later, without the baby he was met by the nurse, who demanded its where- abouts. The young man scratched his head for a moment, then he turned pale, rushed into the desk, hastily unlocked it, and threw up the apron. There lay the baby, slumbering peacefully among the ink bottles, pens, and paper-weights. But the young man doesn't get the baby any more unless they tie a string round his finger.

div.p: " CAPITAL "CHAT.

In lore as in war. Mr. Stanley has succeeded where many others have failed. Nliss Dorothy Tennant has passed for more than one season as the most inveterately deaf young lady of her time to , the appeal of love. Young, beautiful, with great artistic gifts and high intallectual endowments, she has been asked in marriage by several gentlemen— one of them is generally supposed to be the leader of a section, if not a party,in the House of Commons —and now she has finally succumbed to the great explorer.

Miss 'Tennant is known as a constant exhibitor in the Academy, as one of the most welcome guests at every London dinner, and finally, as an intimate friend of Mr. Gladstone and nearly every other remarkable man of her time.

She is considerably above the middle height, has a figure at once vigorous and svelte, and a face per- fectly and beautifully oval. She and her mother and brother—who is also about to abandon single bliss—live in a charming house on Richnumd- terrace, close to the HollSt. of Commons.

According to a Cardiff Correspondent informa- tion has been received in South Wales that Mr. Stanley's wedding to Miss Tennant will take place in Wesiminster Abbey in the last week in Jtrne or the first week in July. Miss Tennant's little nieces, Misses Myers, will attend as bridesmaids and,pages. Mr. Stanley will reside in Richmond-terrace. If he makes further excursions into Africa Miss Tennant will accompany him.

The face of Miss Dorothy Tennant, who is to marry Mr. Stanley, is known to thousands of her fellow countrymen who have never seen her, for it was from sittings which she gave him that Sir J. E. Millais painted the well-known picture, "Yes or No? "—a girl reading a love letter—which has been engraved, and is now to be found everywhere. Miss Tennant lives with her mother in one of the large houses at the eastern end of Richmond-terrace. She is equally at home inart, literature, and politics, and her own room on the ground floor probably contains more photographs and autographs oi con- temporary celebrities than any other apartment in London. It is here that she has discussed the burning question of the day with Mr. Gladstone, Mr. Chamberlain, and a dozen other Cabinet Minis- ters, but in the result she remains a staunch and uncompromising Radical. Herpaintings have been accepted and well hung at Burlington House, but her peculiar forte lies in pen-and-ink drawings of the gamina Of London. She has admirably illustra- ted several magazine articles, and is never happier than when sketching a group of street urchins at play. In this particular lino she has no rival, and as Vice-Queen of 'Central Africa she will doubtless be able to make her husband's books even more attractive than they are at present. Miss Dorothy Tennant is the elder daughter of the late Mr: Charles Tennant, and is also a cousin of Mr. Hamilton- Aide.

Lord Tennyson has, at the request of Mr. Steytler, recited the "Charge of the Light Brigade" and a passage from "Thb Princess" in one of Mr. Edison's phonographs. His son writes to Colonel Gouraud that the tones of his voice, as heard through the tubes, were given back with startling fidelity.

The Queen, wild has not got rid of the bad cold she caught at Darmstadt, was advised not to hold the last Drawing-room. Her Majesty does not throw off her illnesses so easily as when she was younger, and Dr. Reid, who now looks after her, is very careful not tolet her overtire herself, while all are anxious to get her away to Balmoral as soon as possible.

Mrs. William A. Harper, the favourite grand- daughter of Henry Ward Beecher and the grand niece of Mrs. Harriet Beecher-Stowe, is dead. She suffered from toothache and insisted on taking chloroform at the dentist's, which brought on so severe a fit of vomiting that she ruptured a blood- vessel and died a few minutes after. She was a very clever and pretty woman.

Mr. Gladstone will remain just over a fortnight at Hawarden Castle. It has been arranged that during his stay Mr. Gladstone shall be called to give evidence beifore the Committee appointed by the Flintshire County Council to inquire into the best means of giving effect to the Welsh Intermedi- ate Education Act. For this purpose the Committee will hold a sitting at Ilawarden.

Viromens' dress reformers may derive some en- couragement in their crusade against skirts by watching the tendencies of the gymnastic schools. A special costume, for instance, is an essential con- dition of membership of the St. Andrew's Gymnastic and Calisthenic Society. Tunic and knickeibockers of crimson flannel are worn, trimmed with white braid. A white silk belt is added, and the feet are encased in spring shoes with india-rubber soles.

The Emperor of Austria is busy reviewing his troops at Bruck, on the Leitha. Whenever the Em- peror is in Bruek he stays at Count Harrach's Castle. which is surrounded by one of the 'finest parks in the Empire. Count Harrach's hothouses are celebrated for their azaleas, which are now in full bloom, and are visited by excursionists from Vienna during the month of May. The azaleas, with their wealth of pink, white, and bright red blossoms, form (11 picture of rare freshness and beauty.

It does not appear to be generally known, says "Life," that in the recent libel case of Sala v. Furnisa Mr. G. A. Sala's counsel was specially instructed not to ask for damages, as Mr. Sala had no desire to make money out of the affair, and all that the jury were asked through counsel to do in opening the case, and again in the concluding speech for the plaintiff, was to award a sufficient sum over the 40s. paid into court to render Mr. Furniss 'liable for all the costs, thus mulcting him in what was prac- tically a fine of £3OO.

The final farewell of Mr. Sims Reeves will be postponed even longer than has been generally understood. It was originally to have taken place at a concert to be given at the Albert Hall next month, but as Mr. Reeves proposed afterwards to complete his provincial tour the plan was altered, and the Albert Hall concert was put off till the end of October, when Mdme Christine Nilsson was to take part in it. But it seems he cannot complete his provincial tour by October, as he will then have outstanding contracts to sing at certain towns, at which, owing to illness, he has not taken his fare- well.

Wordsworth's cottage at Grasmere is one of the most beautiful spots In a lovely district. It deserves to be saved. Mr. Stopford Brooke and his brother, with Professor Knight of St. Andrews and Mr. Geo. Lillie Craik, are making an appeal that it should be secured, with its orchard and garden, for the modest sum of £650. The promoters aim is to raise the sum by small subscriptions, so that every lover of the poet may contribute, and thus make of Doe Cottage a national memorial to Wordsworth, his sister, and his friends. The idea is a pleasing one, and 80 is the further project of founding a Wordsworth Museum should funds be forthcoming. Mr. Craik is the treasurer.

The "Daily News" says :—During the proceedings which took place in the House of Commons be- tween midnight and four o'clock on Tuesday morn- ing the Closure was ,twice voted once at the instance of Mr. Smith, and the second time at that of the Chancellor of the Exchequer. But three other attempts were made by the supporters of the Government to stop discussien on their important measure—one by Mr. Halsey, a second time by Mr. Aird, and a third time by Mr. Tomlinson. In each case the Chairman of Committees declined to put the question. It will be observed from the Parlia- mentary reportithat at Tuesday morning sitting the Speaker administered a similar rebuff to Mr. Smith when he attempted to closure the debate on the motion giving precedence to the Budget Bill.'

There was an unusually large attendance at Cardinal Manning's annual reception on Tuesday night. From nine to eleven the spacious rooms at the Archbishop's House, Westminster, were thronged with a representative crowd of the Catholic clergy and laity of England. His eminence received them all personally, and addressed to each a few words of appropriate welcome. He was looking well and was in excellent 'spirits, • and round hi a chair were grouped the Bishops of Shrewsbury, Salford, Not- tingham, Middlesbrough, 'Birmingham, Newport, Southwark, Portsmouth, Emmaus, and Amycla. The Marquis of Ripon was prominent, swearing the broad blue ribbon of the Order of the Garter, and was engaged for a considerable time in conversa- tion with the Cardinal Archbishop. An additional interest was given to the gathering by the pre-

sence of several of the pilgrims who have just returned from the Holy Land. The reception should, in the ordinary course of events, have been held in Low-week, but was postponed, as was also 'the annual meeting of the bishops until the present time on account of the pilgrim- age to the Holy Land taking place at the former date.

opportunities for raising crops are certainly not less than the American farmers, for it is notorious that American farm lands are nearly all in the hands of the money thieves, and that in immense numbers of cases mortgages are 'held considerably above the value of the farms. The owning of your own home- stead is fast becoming a thing of the past. Look in the current " Fovum " for Mr. Davis's article on overproduction. 116 says "that the troubles of the farmer are due to the fact that there are altogether too many farms, too many cattle and swine, too many bushels of corn, wheat, rye, oats, barley buck- wheat, and potatoes, too many tons of hay, and too great a production of nearly all othdr farm products for the number of consnmers." I see in this signs that even the export of corn will have its limits. Corn is even being burnt as fuel because it don't pay to export. When once the land question is understood, things may change for the better. In my poor way I tried some years ago,in the columns of the "Examiner," to draw attention to the chief disturbing factor in

div.head: CHIEFLY PERSONAL.
div.p: CHIEFLY PERSONAL.

BY H. Warrithat. I must beg of my good friends in Warrington that they will be just a trifle lenient in their judgment upon me for my seeming neglect. For some time past I have received numerous letters from friends wishing to know a little more touching my own personal affairs. Allow me to say, in this fashion, that I am "real pleased" with the interest thus dis- played in my welfare, and I wish it was within my power to say right here and at once, that I was "doing grand.' I am sorry to say, it is quite the opposite. You all know the circumstances under which 2i years ago 1 left Warrington. I came here to work at my own trade with the promise that I should, as a day wage-man, eam three dollars a day. It was implied that I should haveregular work, and at piece work earn more than three dollars a day. This has all turned out to be untrue. Never lat any time since I came have I been able to work two months at straightforward work. The place is always" shutting down," and I have had to work at ordinary labouring for a dollar and a half per day, and a dollar and six bits-7s. per day. About Christnias we worked double shift for a time; then the double shift worked alternate weeks. The place got full of stock, and on the 26th of this month, April, it shut down. When we shall start work again I don't know, nor does anyone else, and I am a bit inclined to say "I don't care." Now, my friends, you have the whole thing, and pretty brief, I guess. It will be seen from tkis that I have had lots of time for writing; the fact is, I have had no inclination. I wished, and I willed,that I could send word that I was doing well; but my proposing seems to be subject to the disposing of some stronger power, and so for the present I must bide my time. But I should not like it to be thought 1 have not tried to get into something else; for Iknow that is what everybody will be saying and advising. Ad- vertisements without end have been attended to, and I have applied for the highest post, as well as the lowest, even down to street sweeping. You know Carlyle says," All work is holy," so street sweeping must have an aroma about it especially holy. All the same, _ _

NO WORK IS TO i)E HAD. I want to speak out pretty plain on this subject. I want to especially warn a certain class of work- 1 men against coming out here. I do not wish my fellow-countrymen and women to make the mis- take I am afraid I have made, and I may state that what I haveto say applies pretty well to the whole of the United States. The artizan who is doing fairly well at his trade at home, I strongly advise to stay where he is ; especially does this apply to married men with families. Single men, who have no clear ideas as to what a home means, and mar- ried men without families, may do out here, and save money. Every block in the city is made up of sleeping rooms, furnished in all cases, and ready to be let at once. Rent is always demanded for the week or month in advance, whether in private house or in rooms, and the tenant is always at liberty to leave when he likes. So it is clear the working popula- tion is largely what is called transient ; always on the move. I should say, the rooms to which I have referred are cold, comfortless places; no fires in them, nothing of home about them, and every roomer takes his meals at the restaurants, which last are almost as numerous as saloons. This ac- counts for the large amount of patronage received by the saloons, as they are the only places in which a man can spend his time freely, and with comfort. The past winter has been A. REMARKABLY COLD AND WET WINTER, and a long one. The accounts receive.' in the city from all outlying districts have been most drehdful. On one occasion all postal delivery was entirely stopped, and a considerable portion of my own postal matter has been lost. The car tracks and the mountains have been covered with snow to such an extent that all transportation was stopped. The melting of the snow has causekthrough floods, great distress, of which I see friend Winstanley knows something. The usual effects of a hard win- ter have followed ; thousands of men have been out of work; public subscription lists have been opened, and hundreds of men have been employed in the public parks. Daily meetings have been held of the unemployed, at which Socialistic speeches of the pure continental type have been delivered, and leaflets have been issued- in which language, the most extreme, was used. All this has been most re- pugnant to the feelings and policy of the moneyed and employing classes, who have an eye to two things only—the sale of land, land speculation, and the flooding of the labour market, exploiting the working-classes. Just recently 200 Italians have been brought into California. Raw and igno- rant they are, and are to work for $l6 Per month. The Press prints regularly splendid descriptions of vineyards, and raisin farms, describing them as veritable paradises, but not a word is said of the tabour employed, or how it is housed. Letno one be deceived by all this booming business. The labour used all over the States is of the very cheapest, Chinese, Italians, Huns. and Poles. How can the sturdy English artisan compete with these? If a visit is paid to the farms referred to, it will be found that the labour is housed in a style to which the Irish mud cabin is a palace. But what are the effects of it all? Why, that a great proportion of all who land at Castle Gardens locate themselves in the towns, causing the labour question to swell to such a magnitude, that it is now throughout the Stases in a state of open revolt. We have now in this city the greatest strike the Pacific slopes has ever seen. It has lasted two months, and there seems no hope of its ending. Every trade in the city, I may say in the States,is in a state of dis- content, and what we may see on the Ist. May no one knows. In Chicago from £3,000 to 0,000 per day is being lost tbrougk strikes. I know this thing ' is not at all peculiar to the United States but that it is going on throughout the whole of the industrial world, and I only refer to it as applying to America, because I wish to prove to all my readers that-emi- gration to this country is not to be thought of. It is only jumping out if the frying pan into the fire. Of course, my vision'is somewhat limited just ncw, not only am I without the means of gathering in- formation, but, possibly. I am in a sour, discontent- ed mood, and may be viewing things through a glass, darkly; yet I am sure I am right when I say that this American continent is very roue' nearer a social revolution than England is, and a revolution of such magnitude as the world before never saw. Here in this city

div.head: TRADES UNIONS ABOUND.
div.p: TRADES UNIONS ABOUND.

Almost all I;b7u-r--is-united -87,-ia it is almost im- possible for a man to gain employmf nt in any sort of a job, unless he first belongs to the Union, and in some of the Unions an almost prohibitive initia- tion fee is charged, being as high as £2O. Unionism in this case would almost seem to be responsible for the large army of unemployed, but it is really not so, as no trade is so busy but that it can be well supplied with labour. The Unibnists are united almost to a man auto the great necessity for •an eight hours working day. What the results of this will be, if gained, I cannot tell, but I foresee, that if the conditions of life are made more agreeable here, it is more than likely that a new incentive will be given to immigration, and that the present evil state of things will continue, if indeed they are not considerably aggravated. There is, to be sure, a strong feeling against the continuance of the influx of foreign labour, and steps are being taken for its discontinuance,but what hopes can there be of suc- cess, when all power is in the hands of capitalists, when labour is not at all represented in this free country, as it is in monarchical and aristo- cratic England when the working-man, at every election, however important or unimportant it may be, delivers himself over body and soul, for a raw of pottage, to the political boss? There is a marked decrease in the immigra- tion figures, but such as they are they should be considered by Englishmen. In 1881 Germany sent here 210,485. in 1889 95,947, a decrease of 114,538. These figures prove that the Germans are aware of the tate of things here. In 1881 Eng- land and WaTes sent 66,204, Ireland 72,342, in all 136,46; in 1889, altogether 122,885, England's share being more by 42,000, and Ireland less by the same number. Now, ) WHAT ARE ENGLISHMEN DOING?

Or what are they rot doing? First, they are neg- lecting to keep themselves posted with the state of things out here, and next they are allowing their nation's best bone and sinew to come out here, to this land which lives under as injurious land laws as any other country in the world. Arrangements are made.by,Englishmen to bring out h'ere to Cali' fornia 200 of the best and well-to-do English farmers. These men will locate in this State, and will, no doubt, prosper, by employing cheap labour, but why should they not prosper at home? Their

div.head: EVERLASTING_ LABOUR QUESTION.
div.p: THE EVERLASTING_ LABOUR QUESTION.

My position is, that so long that Workmen allow the present economical conditions to hold they must abide by their results, and that strikes are only partial palliatives and not remedies. - There- foe it follews that as air is free, so water should be free, and land should be owned by the people and not by the individual. How I have been sneered at by wiseacres for preaching this doctrine years ago! And how often have I in the columns of the 1" Examiner " said the following, which appeared in the columns of a local neutral of yours of April 9th: —" The French work this same coal bed, without let or hindrance from anyone, because, happily, in France the minerals belong to the State, But in England the minerals belong to the landlord, and his permission and his terms must be asked before an ounce of the discovered coal can be brought into use. It is thus the great industries of England have been throttled and handicapped in their corn- petition with foreign traders. We are in conse- quence a century behind our neighbours across the Channel in findi,ng this coal, and now we have found it we have to go cap in hand for permission to get it, and may be refused except on terms that make it utterly impossible to work it." But a great change is coming over the industrial world. We have been slow in realising what Carlyle meant in " Sartor Resartus." It must be read afresh, and I beg of all workmen to get the book; it will give fresh life to the labour movement. Get hold of• Ruskin and read in the' Crown of Wild Olives," the chapter on "Traffic," I should like to quote but must forbear. I Must leave this subject, but how much should I
like to refer to recent striking utterances of the Pope and Cardinal Manning, and to the speech in Prance on the German Emperor's doings. All must be left so that I may close with just a reference to

div.head: OUR BIG RARTINFARR..
div.p: OUR BIG RARTINFARR..

It happened in the night, as usual. About 3.45 we were awakened rather roughly by the bedstead playing antics on the room floor. The wife was shook right down in bed; in fact I don't know whether she was not shaken out of bed. The first thing I knew after the shaking was that she stood at the beside shaking, too, calling out, " Oh, for God's sake, Harry, let us get out of this country." I am disposed to take most things just now, either stoically,or" Mark Tapleyish." I don't see any differ- ence between the net results of a tidal wave, an earthquake, or being starved to death. Therefore, lam resigned, merely asking "What next?' In some districts considerable damage was done. In the city, the cracking of walls, upsetting of orna- ments, and in the hotels the crowding of corridors with slightly draped roomers were the chief inci- dents. I see, in this morning's papers, that an Orphanage sheltering ninety-six orphans was laid in ruins, and an appeal is being made for money to rebuild. It is only an insignificant notice in the corner of the paper; too great notice might put a stop to booming. We are now, holding a family council as to the advisability of leaving this part of the country, Seattle is spoken of—a thousand miles away—l don't know how it will be. 810, Bay-st., San Fransisco, April 29th, 1890.

div.head: QUEEN AND THE COMMANDER-
div.p: THE QUEEN AND THE COMMANDER-
SHIP-IN-CHIEF.

With reference to the statement in the " Manchester Guardian" that the Queen desires the retention of the Commandership-in-Chief as an appanage of the Crown, and with a view to the appointment of the Duke of Connaught, we (" Daily Chronicle '') have again to say, as we said some' weeks ago, that her Majesty does desire the retention of the office, but she does not wiDh it to be held by a Prince of the blood.
PROJECTED ROYAL VISIT TO IRELAND.

It is understood that the Prince of Wales has signified his acceptance of the invitation of Sir Edward Cecil Guinness, Bart., to pay a visit of a strictly private char- acter to Dublin, and to be present at the Whitsuntide meeting of the celebrated Baldoyle Races on the 26th and 27th inst. His Royal Highness will also be present at the contest for the Irish Tennis Championship, which will be held in the splendid grounds attached to Sir Edward's residence in St. Stephen's-green, Dublin.

div.head: SUPPOSED MURDER OF A WOMAN.
div.p: SUPPOSED MURDER OF A WOMAN.

On Saturday evening, at Mitcham, Surrey, the body of a woman calling herself Eliza Beadle, supposed to be the wife of a man named Nightingale, but who cohabited with a labourer named George Bowling, was found in the house of the latter with her head smashed in, it is supposed with a hammer which was found in the room. Bowling was subsequently arrested on suspicion. He was charged at Croydon, on Monday, inorniag4 with the murder of Eliza Nightingale, of Mitcham. Prisoner ad- mitted his guilt before the magistrates, and was remanded.
WRECK OF A STEAMER.-LOSS OF SIX LIVES.

A Lloyd's telegram from Belfast, on Saturday, reports that the steamer Harold, of Hull, from Santandar for Ayr, after getting ashore on the Butter Plady, in the morning floated off and proceeded on her voyage ; but when in Cloughev Bay she began settling down, and eventually foundered. Six lives were lost. The remainder of the crew were picked up by the steamer Telegraphic. A Derry correSpondent states that on Saturday evening the Belfast steamer Telegraphic arrived there with part of the crew of the Harold. The Harold had a crew of 17 hands. As the steamer sank -the boilers exploded. One of the rescued men, Angus Campbell, of Portri, Skye, died from shock and exhaustion. Frank Edgar, fireman, sustained a serious injury to his head. The captain, Smith, was also hurt. The men drowned in- cluded the first mate, Brunton, of Hull; and the first engineer, John Ace, of

div.head: RAILWAY COLLISION AT , ARDWICK.
div.p: RAILWAY COLLISION AT , ARDWICK.

A railway collision, causing injury to ten or 12 per- sons, and great consternation amongst all the passengers affected by ittook place soon after ten o'clock on Mon- day morning between London-road and Ardwick Stations, on the Manphester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire system. A goods engine, and brake standini, at the Ruxton-roadrjtuiction were run into by the 10r-10 pass- enger train fiom Lendon-road to Woodley and Hydet and the brake was thrown off the line. The travellers by the passenger train were much shaken, one woman named Mary Duggan, of 22, Redland-lane, Hyde being seriously injured on the chest: The line was blocked for about an hour, during which time the service was con- ducted on one set of metals. All the passengers were able to continue their journey by other trains, with the exception Mrs. Duggan, who was badly injured, and was at once removed to the Manchester Royal Infirmary.

div.head: WELSH SCHEME OF HOME RULE.
div.p: A WELSH SCHEME OF HOME RULE.

In order to promote Welsh Home Rule, Mr. Gee, chair- man of the Denbighshire County Council, proposes a detailed scheme In the current number of his vernacular paper. He demands Home Rule all round. He declares this can be accomplished without imperilling the interests of either England, Scotland, Ireland or Wales. He sug- gests that each country should have its own Parliament with exclusive control over its own domestic affairs, in- cluding education, religion, preservation of order, and the land laws, and such other matters as pertain to each separate country. Each country should possess one house only, elected by direct vote or the people. The Welsh senate should meet at Aberystwith, the Scotch at Edinburgh, the Irish at Dublin, and the English in LDn- don. The Imperial Parliament would continue to meet in London to discuss and control general affairs, and also foreign policy. Members would be elected by the four countries, together- with a number of representatives from the colonies.

div.head: LIVING LEGA.QZ-.
div.p: A LIVING LEGA.QZ-.
GEO. MANVILLE FENN; ,distior of " Dutch the Diver," " The Foundry Belle," cfc.,
CHAPTER %%ILL

817CCESS. Tux visito-- to Humphreys' establishment on business matters of hill:min crouched there listening, but it was a false alarm, so, creeping tothe table, he opened a drawer, took out a key, with which he opened a small stand, wherein were a decanter, glasses, and biscuits. "Not drugged for the benefit of burglars," he said with a half-laugh, as he poured out and drained a couple of glasses, the wine glistening in the light docile by the half-turned down gas. Refreshed thereby, he crept with his old tactics ink the hall, where, setting down his heavy bag, he listenei for a moment or two, and then slipped off his over- shoes, stripped off the jersey shirt, and kicked off the trousers. Then the string of the cap was broken and the crape and a great false beard pulled off, a cup- board opened, and a hat and overcoat taken there- from the transformation being as rapid as it was complete. "So far so good," he muttered; and, gathering up his disguise, he bore it into an inner office, opened the door of a large stove, thrust all in, struck a match, applied it, and closed the door. A dull, roaring sound ensued, showing that the place had been prepared with some inflammable; and, this done, he crept back after closing the door, threw a railway rug over his arm, picked up the heavy bag, and stepped to the side entrance, but stopped with his hand upon the fastening, for he could hear voices outside. "Has he given the alarm?" he thought; and, setting down the bag, he ran quickly up to the manager's room, but all was still—no, there was a low, moaning noise. He ran down as softly as a oat, and listened at the side door. Murmur—murmur—murmur. There were two people talking for certain, and he must wait. This was the most crucial task of all. The robbery had been effected, the two guandians of the place die abled, if not killed; the treasure was at his feet, and all he had to do was to step outside and retreat to a place of safety with a handsome fortune, while now that all was ready, there were a couple of gossiping people in the way, stopping him with their silly chatter. He cursed them bitterly in his heart, and stood gnawing his lip, and thinking of how often it was that some great, deeply-laid scheme had been defeated by a miserable trifle. He could have stamped upon the floor in his rage as the buzz of voices still went on; for at any moment the old manager might recover sufficiently to give the alarm. The porter was safe enough, but the effect of the chloroform might wear off at any moment. He listened, trying to make out what was said, but in vain; and then he started, for there was the sound of a fall upstairs. followed by a feeble hammering upon the floor. The manager had evidently struggled from the bed to the floor, and was trying to make himself heard. "Ho will get to the bell directly," the man muttered; " and then—Thank heaven !" It was a curious expression this last for one to make whose lasthour had been employed in what might prove to have been murder as well as robbery; but it did not strike him who spoke as absurd, so taken up was he with the fact that there were footsteps on the pavement out- side, and that the voices were growing more distant. "I shall do it yet," he cried, joyfully, ai he stood in the darkness listening and battling with the dread he felt at hearing the beating noise still continuing from the manager's bedroom. His hand was upon the catch of the door, and he longed to open and flee, but he was constantly deterred by the feeling that every- thing depended upon his keeping cool and finishing his enterprise with patient care. The slightest slip now would destroy the whole of his work, and a token of haste draw the attention of the first policeman on the beat. He waited minute after minute, every one of which seemed to be drawn out to an interminable length, and still he dared not go. The rest of the task seemed easy as compared to this. Suddenly, as he stood there, with the perspiration streaming from his face, there was the creaking noise of a bell-wire, followed by the loud jangling of a bell below, and directly after, faintly heard, the ringing of a bell up stairs. The manager was reviving, and his next step would be to crawl to the window, break the panes, and summon help. There was not a moment to lose. It was now or never. But for those miserable gossipers be would have been far away by now. Catching up the bag, be softly opened the side door, listened for a moment or two to the sounds without, and a cry upstairs, stepped out, closed the door softly, and walked away, reaching the end of the lane just as attic door was opened and a couple of trembling women began to descend to answer the bell, for the robbery of Mr. Middlecombe's patent vault had been successfully carried out, and the firm of Humphrey and Company were the poorer by many thousand pounds.

div.head: CHAPTER XXIV.
div.p: CHAPTER XXIV.
A TERRIBLE BUSINEBB.

Rtrrn Lima had gone to her room at Mark s stern command, to seat herself by her bed and lay her head upon her pillow, weeping bitterly at what had taken place. "What will be think of me 7—what will he think of me?" keptrepeating itself, as she placed her hands to her throbbing brow, and the tears fell faster and faster still. She heard the door close as Mark went out, und waited, listening intently, as she felt sure that be had gone outside to walk up and down so as to meet his brother upon his return; and she knew that there would be an angry quarrel that she could not prevent. "Poor Martin! she sighed at last, and, weary with waiting, she went to bed, feeling that even if she heard a serious quarrel between the brothers she would not dare to interfere. But it was not to sleep, for, with every nerve attent, she could hear the sl,ghtest sound, either in the house or passing in the street, so that it almost pained her to listen, and yet she felt that she must. Again and again she started up, fancying that she could hear the click of a key in the latch, but after painful listenin g she knew that she was deceived, and lay down once more. That last was unmistakeable though; there was the click of the latch, the faint cracking of the door. Then came a quick step on the oilcloth, and the stairs creaked as some one ascended. " Martin," she whispered to herself; and she lay listening to the opening of his door, the noise he made in kicking off his boots, and then his door closed, and she could hear the hurried moving about of the young man in his room. . _ _

Not many minutes after, there was the click of the latch once more and the noise in Martin's bedroom suddenly ceased. Then menially illustrating the sounds she heard, Ruth saw Mark enter the hall, close the door, calmly divest himself of his overcoat, and after standing thoughtfully for a few moments coma slowly upstairs to his room. Ruth echoed the sigh he uttered, as she bitterly felt the unhappiness of the house in which her lot was cast, and wondered whether she could win Martin back to a better way. The hours passed, and sleep came not to visit her eyes. Day broke, and she lay watching the dim light stealing through her blind, and listening to the rattle of the carts and cabs to and from the great station near at hand. At last, weary with lying sleepless, she rose and dressed, intending to go down and fetch a book, for it was now five o'clock.

Hardly, however, had she come to this determina- tion than she was startled by the loud ringing of the front door bell, and, going to the window, she was just in time to hear Mark's thrown up; and directly after he was in conversation with a policeman, who had evidently just alighted from a hansom cab. "Have you got a doctor?" "Yes, sir; and the first thing he said was your name. That was all; but the housekeeper told me where you lived." "Down directly," exclaimed Mark, and in a very few minutes he was descending, meeting Ruth on the landing. "You up, Ruth?" he said, coldly. "Yes, Mark; I have not slept all night," she said, looking piteously in his face. "What is the matter?"

" Trouble at the office," he said, coldly. "Here Martin get hp quickly. The office has been robbed„ and A4.ll:Dlopstock half killed." There was the sound of some one leaping out of bed. "Never! Impossible ! I'll be dressed directly, Mark. Are you going down?" "Yes."

"Don't go without me." Mark descended the stairs, closely followed by Ruth, who asked, with beating heart, whether she could do anything to be of service. "No, my child," he said.more kindly, as he sav her disturbed looks; "only go and comfort poor Miss Rlopstock, and pray heaven that matters be not so bad for our Door old friend."

He admitted the policeman and a brief conver- sation ensued. "Are you ready, Martin?" " Yes," was the reply; and the young man, looking pale and excited, came hurrying down, nodded shortly at Ruth, took his hat, and the brothers joined the policeman, whom they accompanied to the office, which was in the occupation of three more constables, one of whom led the way up to Mr. Klopstock's room. "I was on duty, sir, and as I reached the end,pf the lane I heard a window smash, and there was the poor old gentleman's bare arm stuck out and waving to me. I called out to him to know if he could come down and open the door, and the arm went in again; and though I knocked and rang there was no answer. Then another of our men came up, and we were talk- ing of having the door broken open when we heard a noise of some one falling down-stairs, and then the door was opened by one of the women, and we went up, broke in the bed-room door, and found the poor gentleman lying under the window, bleeding and fainted away." By this time they had reached the manager's bed- room, to find him lying in his bed, his head bandaged, and a ghastly pallor in his face. A surgeon was sitting by him, and Mark asked if he might speak. He asked this question in a whisper, but the old man heard it add opened his eyes, closed them, shuddered, and began to mutter. "This is a terrible business, Klopstoek," sail Mark, softly. "I hope you are not much hurt." "See the place—search," he said, in a whisper. "Robbery." "Have you examined the place ? " said Mark, turn- ing to the police. " Net wuch, sir. Tbere's nothing wrong down- stairs: not a door broken op -a or a drawer touched as far as we can see at present." - -

- Mark went straight to the drawer where the keys were kept, and pulled it open. "The keys are not here,' he said, hoarsely. "Keys—my keys,' groaned the old man. " Help ! " "The keys have been taken," exclaimed Mark; " perhaps he can give us a clue. Can you tell us how it was, Ktopstock ?" "No," said the surgeon, inteTo,ing. "He must be kept quiet. He has alrtady told the t olice-sergeant cli he could, and you must now leave him." "What keys does he mean, sir ?" said the sergeant, looking at him sharply. "Of the strong vault. Let us go i'own and see." As Mark left the room, he saw that the old man's eyes were open. and that he was watching him in a euri- ouely excited manner, his eyes tollowing him until he disappeared. Outside Mark was made acquainted with all the police knew. On descending to the manager's room the decanter and glass upon the table caught his eye.. "Not usual, eh, sir ?" said the sergeant, who was watching him eagerly. "Oh, no. Those have beeß taken from the cellaret," said Mark. "I do not see anything else moved. The strong room does not seem to have been opened." "Oh! that's the strong room, is it, sir ?" said the sergeant, examining the door. "If it has been opened it's been locked up again, and the keys are gone. But before we go any further, sir, who sleeps in this place of a night ?" "The housekeeper and a maid upstairs; the under porter, Edward downstairs." "Yes, sir, that's what the maids say; but Edwards was called away last night, and by the old gentleman's orders, your porter—Hall—was fetched, and was to sleep here." "That looks bad," cried Martin. "He was sent away for drunkenness, and was very insolent and threatening to my brother here." "But :here is he, sir ?—that's it. He's not here. The maids say he went to bed, and that's all they know."

"lit looks worse," said Martin. " Ah, well, I daresay we shall find him when we want him," said the sergeant. "Have you searched the house? The poor fellow may be lying hurt." "Yes, sir ; he isn't here," said the sergeant. "We've been everywhere. Bless your heart, sir, it's all as clear as can be. Case lies in a nutshell. It's plain enough. The cld gentleman was upset by some one who knew all about the place, and who must have been in wait- ing, for I don't see a lock forced. No outsider could have done it." Mark gazed thoughtfully about, and Martin peered here and there, while the sergeant tried the drawers. "What we hive to find out is whether the strong vault has been entered," said Mark. "Much cash there, sir?' "A very heavy sum, as it happened." "Yes, sir, as it happened," said the sergeant, wink- ing to himself. "Curious how these robberies take place when a lot of money happens to be in the safe." The sergeant went on peering about till his attention was taken up by the fireplace, in which a quantity of dyed willow-shavings had been placed, and some of this seemed to have been dragged out. "What's been going on here," said the sergeant. "Anyone tried to get up the chimney ?" He took the poker and raised the register, when a dull tinkling noise was heard. "Hallo!" "That stove has not been used for some time," said Auk. .

"No, sir, so it seems," said the sergeant, quietly,, "Just lay hold here, Jones." The man addressed came forward, and they dreii the register stove right out of the setting, and there lel the keys, half buried in a heap of soot. "Your safe's empty, sir, you may take your oath,' said the sergeant. Those are the keys, certainly," exclaimed Mark. 'That is the first key; never mind the rest. Here, let me." He opened the door that led down to the vault, and descended, followed by the others. "What's that?" exclaimed Mark. They stopped to listen, for a strange tapping noise tell upon their ears. Mark took a step forward and unlocked, one after the other, the doors of the strong room till the last was thrown open, and by the light of the outer gas jet, they could see the kneeling figure of the porter supporting' himself by one hand clinging to the handle of a drawer, a pocket knife, with which be had been tapping the door, was held in the other hand. "Good heavens! he is here," cried Mark. "Then we've got our bird without putting salt on his tail," said the sergeant. "Why, he must have locked himself in by mistake, sir. Here, hallo, my hearty. Where's the swag ?" The porter turned a bewildered face to those before him, gazing from one to the other, and placing his hand to the back of his head, which was bleeding, and they now saw a little pool of blood on the steel floor, where the poor fellow had lain. "Nonsense, constable !" cried Mark; "he must have been locked up here." "Then it must have been by his pals," said the sergeant, stubbornly. " Dessay they quarrelled about the plunder, and he got locked in while they went off. Make a good witness. Here, lay bold some one. Let's get him out. Jones, ask the doctor to step down. Hall was carried up to the manager's room and laid upon the couch, where Martin assisted the surgeon in his ministrations, Mark proceeding with the sergeant to the examination of the safe, Martin following almost directly after. "Do you know, sir, what there should be here?" "Not exactly, without reference to the books, but near enough to see if there has been anything taken.* "Oh, there has been something taken," said the sergeant, gruffly. "That chap didn't get that crack on the head for nothing." "Why he must have heard them, sergeant, and came to pretect the property of the firm," said Mark, eagerly. Very likely, sir," said the man, drily. "There's no knowing what unaccountable things some people won't do." Mark went on with his examination,opening drawer after (hewer, and door after door. "Pocket-books slit open—note cases gone. Good heavens, sergeant, there has been a heavy sum taken in notes and securities, and—one, two, three, yes I think six bags of sovereigns." "Stop a moment, sir, I'll put that down," said the sergeant, tugging out a memorandum-book. 'There is a note-case gone with about eleven thou- sand pounds in Bank of England notes." "And put that down, sir," said the sergeant. "May be useful. Well, sir, what next ?" "I cannot tell now without careful examination." said Mark, wiping his forehead. "That's quite enough to begin upon, sir," said the 1 sergeant. "First thing is to get the numbers and stop all those notes." I "I shoeld say quite fifteen thousand pounds have been stolen," continued Mark, looking at his brother. "In a most convenient shape," said the sergeant. "Now sir, what's your opinion ?" Mark seemed stunned at the extent of the misfor- tune, and gazed from one to the other in a bewildered Way. "I cannot say," he replied, for his brain was full of horrible suspicions. "Well, air, it's plain enough that it was done by some one quite at home in the place. Eli! What say, Smith?" . Here's a bit of a patch on the wall," said the con- stable with them who bad been peering about with the aid of a candle, obtained from the white and shiver- ing maids; "and here's another on the floor. Yes, and, look here, there's a couple of smudges along close by the door and inside here."

"Brityvo, Smith, my active and intelligent member or our noble force. You'll be promoted yet. Oh yes, of course," he continued, examining the smudges. " You are about right, sir. Master porter heard em up .to their games, and came down. Whoever it was, give him one, and he fell up against the wall there, and then on the floor, and then they dragged him in by his legs. Look where his head smeared the floor. What's that ?" "Kitchen poker," said Smith. " Ah, I'll be bound to say that's what he brought and didn't use. Why, here's a little special coa- st able's staff too, loaded with lead. That belong to the place, sir ?" "No," said Mark. "I never saw it before." " What have you got here, sir ?" "Two buttons," said Martin. "Busted off his clothes, sir, as they dragged him im I'm beginning to think there was two in the job. Well I say it was some one belonging to the place." "Or who has belonged to the place," said Mark, sl- eitedly, for his horrible suspicion was gaining tr, eagth• "That's right, I dare say, sir," replied the sergeant. " We'll see the list of discharged servants." The man looked very hard at Mark; then be glanced at Aladin before suggesting that the safes should be lockea up and sealed. After which they ascended to the manager's room, to find that Samson Hell viss perfectly insensible, and that the doctor was looking
I

grave. "Concussion of the brain," he said. "The men must have been struck down by a tremendous blow in the face, and his head has come in contact with the floor with terrible violence." "Then that locks up a lot of information," said the sergeant, thoughtfully; and, in accordance with the sergeant's request, two of his men carried the porter down to the bedroom in the basement, where the set- geant had a fresh look round, but saw nothing to take his attention. After this Mr. Klopstock's room was revisited,. where he too new was perfectly insensible. to, "That's the aggravating part of our business, sir, said the sergeant, as they descended to the counting- house. "Those two have got all we want to know locked up in their insensible heads, and till they C eak we've got to work in the dark. Ah, well : dare say we shall make it out yet. The worst of it is that, while we are waiting, him who planned this little job is getting away. I'll justhave another look round,' he said, abruptly. Mark went to the manager's room, and wrote off to the members of the firm, and to the principal clerks, then, with Martin's help, he made out a list of the stolen notes, and sent it to the bank for them to be stopped- One way and another he worked so hard, that st the regular time for commencing business it could g° on as usual, the outside world knowing nothing of the robbery till a brief notice appeared in the evening papers. Meanwhile the police had examined and re-examiood the premises, only finding one thing, besides Soo* fresh ashes in a stove, to give them a clue to the offender, and that clue was carefully taken to the cho , office, without a word reaching the ears of Mark, only heard from the sergeant a repetition of his belief that the crime was committed by some one who bea been concealed in the building, while the tempoter,YA manager had to report to the firm, when they show', arrive, that their losses amounted to nineteen thoussno pounds, which ought to have been lying in safety 10 I bank, but which their old-fashioned prejudice insisteo upon being kept in their own strong vault, for vali`'b they had quite lately paid so heavy a sum. (To his continued.)

div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four. PRIVATE Blus.—The Manchester Ship Canal (Tidal Openings, &c,) Bill, the Seacombe, Hoylake, and Deeside Railway Bill, and the Ribble Navigation Bill were read a third time and passed. SOCIALISTIC LmoistArioN.—Lord WEMYSS called atten. , tion to the Socialistic legislation of the last two sessions, and dealt with the whole subject under three heads : the Socialism of legislation, the Socialism of the schools, and the Socialism of the streets.—Lord SALISBURY said the noble earl had brought before the House an extraordin- ary mixture, including projects utterly ridiculous and alisurd and others decidedly beneficial. He believed that , If Socialistic schemes could once be brought into action they would provoke so much indignation that very little would be heard of them afterwads.—The subject then dropped, MElacnesT SHIPPING Bna..—The Merchant Shipping 4etB Amendment Bill passed through Committee. HOUSE OF LORDS.—ThensmY.

The House rn-t at fur The L•6l Chancellor took his Seat at a quarter past four o'clock. BILLS ADVANCED.—The Reformatory Schools Bill and the Juvenile Offenders Bill passed through their Com- mittee stage on recommitment.--Earl BEAUCHAMP said that before the bills passed through the House he wished to draw attention to the great labour which had been bestowed on these bills, a fact likely to be lost sight of since these matters had been relegated to Grand Coln- inittees.—The Marquis of Salisbury said that the bills in Committee received a more searching and critical examination than they, received in their lordships' house.
MERCHANT SHIPPING LAWS.—The Merchant Shipping Acts Amendment Bill was read a third time. The House adjourned at five o'clock until Thursday the sth June. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Tuunsnex. _ . . . . .

The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. Qunsnoss, &c.—Sir JAMES FERGUSON, answering a question, said that the countries entitled to the benefits of the "most favoured nation" treatment would par- take in the reduction of import duties conceded by Greece to this country, but the articles in the Greek tariff selected for reduction were those which were im- ported in the largest measure from England. Mr. Rams, referring to a complaint by Mr. S. Smith as to the growth of the betting telegram system, stated that the Post Offiee could not discriminate between the different classes of messages. Mr. Hastings brought under notice a resolution passed by the blickrock Com- missioners reflecting on the conduct of Mr. Sexton in a committee dealing with a Dublin Corporation Bill. He declared the imputations made to be entirely without foundation, SirJ. MOWBRAY concurred in this, and Mr. SMITH said he thought the House would agree that Mr. Sexton had acted with the most scrupulous sense of honour and entirely in the public interest. ,THE BUDGET, BILL.—The House proceeded to consider the Budget Bill as amended in Committee, and the report having been agreed to, it went into Committee of Supply on Civil Service and Revenue Department Estimates. Mr. E. BECKETT asked for an assurance that the terri- tories in Africa now within the sphere of British influence should not be handed over to Germany. Sir. JAMES FERGUSSON said that answers could only be given when negotiations were completed. He hoped we should not be behindhand in Africa any more than we had been elsewhere, but we must not talk as if we had an inde- feasible right to every spot of the coqntry where colonis- ing enterprise might be successful. We were delling 'With a friendly Power, and negotiations were preceeding on terms ormutual respect and confidence. SUPPLY, &c.—The House afterwards went into Com- mittee of Supply; and, later on, a further account of the Civil services and revenue departments estimates. The Working Classes' Dwellings Bill passed through Com- mittee. The House adjourned at,12•23.

div.head: SUPPER I' TH' DARK.
div.p: A SUPPER I' TH' DARK.
BY GEORGB Huts.

It took but a short time to get the entire company some refreshment; and after George Walton had given a few minutes' uninterrupted attention to his supper, praised Roger's cooking, and thanked him heartily, be was as ready to tell the tale as the others were to hear it. "Aw've no deawt," 'he began, "Yo o' know owd Sammy Flutterton, an' wod a quare o ard stick he is." "Aye, weel enough," was the universal response. "An some on yo may know 'at he's a bit near seeted, an' terble gaumless." "Aye." "Well, he's a terble chap for hevin' milk an' looaf to his supper, an' to his dinner, too, for thact matter. He'd hey 1(1 to every meal iv his wife would mek id him, just because he's sich a likin for it hisser ; an' he ne'er thinks a wod th' wife an' childer wants, iv heyeds his milk an' looaf. . .

tine Setterda neet when in hed bin too wet to go th' teawn, an' hoo hed'nd mich meyt to cook off, his wife wer lamentin' o'er wod a poor dinner they'd hey for Sunda'. " Wod's ta think we'd better rayley hey for th' dinner, Sammy?" hoe said, "th' shop 'll be shuttin' up varra soon." "0," said Sammy, quite thowtless, "dinner, does ta say: owt at o'll do. Ged an extra quart, an' let's ha'e some milk an' looaf I" "The dule tek th' milk an' /ooaf," hoo said, "an' thee, too: for tha'rt milk an' looaf mad." An' hoo went eawt an' welly spent up i' butcher's meyt, for hoo wer determined to hey summat fresh, for once. Sammy kicked up a row, an' he wod'nd give in oather, for he'd some ov his favourite taMe at top ov his meyt an' pratoes th' day after. Heawever, that's nod my main point. Th' doo 'at aw wer laughin' o'er happened one neet last wcek. Sammy lied bin workin' terble late av a neet for some time, an' last Thorsda' neet be corn hooam as late as ever. Th' wife an' childer hed o gone to bed, but he hed a latch key, so he leet hisser into th' heawse. When he geet into th' kitchen he felt onto th' cornice for th' matches, but he could find nooan, so he seet him deawn to ged his supper i' tl,' dark, or at leeast bi wod bit o' leet he could ged off th' fire. As usual, he tow'd th' wife to leeave him his 'leawance (allowance) o' milk an' looaf, an he snap- ped howd ov a basin off th' oven, geet a spoon, an' seet to wark. Bein' a bit dry, he took a good two- o'-thre' spoonfuls o' t' "milk " at fost. "Dell id," he said to hissel, "these farmers are geddin' awful for adulteratin' their milk. This here tastes o' nowt, unless it's chalk." So, disgusted wi' th' "milk," he tackled th' "bread." Bi gew, thad wer woss nor ever! He could noather chew id, nor teetir id, thongh*he'd some rare owd tusks ov his own. At last he geet gradely mad, an' he went to th' bottom o' th' stairs an' sheawted to th' wife: "Ek, lass, are ta wakken?"

_ "Aye," hoo sheawted back. " Well, wod th' name o' fortin (fortune) he ta med mi for mi supper?" "Milk an' looaf, to be sure!" hoo sheawted ageean. "Are ta tekkin' a fresh torn at last--is thad nod reet for tha, like?" "Is id hectum as like I Th' milk's med o' chalk arf watter, an' as for th stuff 'at should be bread— whey, it's like tripe a bit, but tougher than leather!" "Eh, lad, tha'rt a weary foo'. Aw med a bonny set o' misel' when aw wed thee, for tha't to' gsum- less to be trusted i' thi own heawse hi thisel. Wodever hes to bin suppin'—pisun (poison) or wod ? ' Wheer dud ta ged thi milk an boat fro?" "Off th' oven,' sheawted Sammy. " Well, aw'm sure aw could swear aw put id o' th' boiler, an' nod, o' th' oon," hoo sheawted ageean. Sammy looked across th' kitchen, an', sure enough, there waur another basin o' summat on th' boiler. He med a rush for 't, examined id bi th' fire, an' tasted on 't. )3i gum, id wer gradely milk an' loon! this time! He rushed back to th' bottom o' th' stairs, an' sheawted' up ageean. "Whey, lass, th' stuff is on th' boiler after o'. There wer quateness for a minnat ; Sammy's wife wer studyin' ; but heo soon sooarted th' mistake eawt, an' sheawted ageean, wi' a vengeance. "Eh, Sammy, tha'rt a bonny gret leatherheyd, iv ever there waur one! What's ta think tha's bin tryin' to eyt ?" ' Nay," said Sammy, " heaw do aw know ?" " Tha owt to know.," hoo said; an' then boo brast eawt laughin' Sammy wer gedelin' his ' paddy ' up, " Aw'll eyt ray shirt iv aw domed gi'e thee a good hidin,' lady, soon." "Sammywull!" hoo sheawted, "tha's bin comin' varra near eytin' thi shirt oready. Tha'a bin doom' thi level lest to eyt thi own collars an' fronts!" " Heaw the thunder does ta mek thad eawt ?" he axed,in a voyce 'at stopped her laughin; an' changed her tune a bit. "Whey," hoo said, "aw wer starchin,' does ta see, an' aw missed two collars an' fronts, an' a pair o' cuffs. Aw recollect neaw clappinem onto th' oven th' starch, an' forgeddin' owt abeawt 'em. Aw forgeet 'em entirely; aw rayley dud, Sam, but it's thi own collars an' fronts tha's bin eytin' as sure as I tha'rt wick !"

• " Well, George," said Captain Lol, "seem' as it's yo cis hes towd th' tale, aw con just manage to he- lieve it, but only just. Iv id wer onybody else, aw couldn'd ha' swallowed id." "Whey, wodever for ?" inquired Young Turpin ; "aw could believe as Sammy hed swallowed an odd collar or cuff, iv George bed said snoa, for aw know Sammy ov owd. He's a meawth like a coyl pit; an' he ne'er chews his meyt—he chucks (Orates) id deawn wi' th' fork or spoon just th' same as iv he wer eh uckin' coyls onto th' boiler fire at his work:, "Yo may ayther believe id or let id alooan whichever yo like;" said George, genially, "id matters 'nowt to me. But it is true: ax Sammy's wife; hoo'll tell id yo better nor aw've done—a lot." "Bother his wife nooan," said Roger, "but th' fost as meets Sammy just ax him heaw long id is sin' he bed his supper i' th' dark, an' then watch his face. Yo'll soon see heaw he teks id. . . . Neaw then, pass the ball around, lads—who'll give us another crack' as good as th' last ?"—From "The Preston Guardian."

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 24, 1890

Fashion," published by Messrs. Houlston arid Sons, of London, contains a large number of fashion illustrations, in addition to three coloured plates. Amongst the articles we have "Novelties for the Day," "Society and fashion," "Hairdressing in Ancient Greece," "New Mantles and Millinery," " Pramings photographs," "Round the London shops," " How to wear your clothes," etc. "Pirated Poems "is the title of a reprint of an old book found on a book stall. It is published by Messrs. Howe and Co., of London ,with a note to the author inti- mating that if he can be found and make good his claim a share will, be given him of any profits received from the publication. The poems are evidently the woik of a clever and cultured writer, who has seen a good deal of the world, and especially of its seamy side. He has a gift of humour which is peculiarly his own, as will be seen from the following short poem called " Mixed." Within my earthly temple there's a crowd; There's one of us that's humble, one that's proud; There's one that's broken-hearted for his sins ; And one who, unrepentant, sits and grins; There's one who loves his neighbour as himself ; And one who cares for nought but fame and pelf;

From much corroding care —I ehould he free ; - If once I could determine which te Me. The little volume is in cloth, and is published at the low price of 6d. It should have an extraordinary run. Amongst the illustrated papers in the "Ladies' Trea- sury" for this month we have "The Land of Gold and Sheep," "Mount Blanc," and "The Eiffel Tower." There are, besides, articles on ancient and modern art, gardening, cookery, pastimes, chess, &c. "Sir Charles Halle" is the title of a biographical sketch of the great musician, which is published by Mr. John Heywood. It gives an interesting and sympathetic account of Sir Charles's career, the sketch being the substance of articles that have appeared in the "Man- chester Weekly Times." They Will, no doubt, be accept- able to musical readers in this permanent form. People on holiday thoughts intent cannot do better than obtain a list of Mr. Heywood's illustrated guides. They will be astonished to find how much can be given for a penny, and how really fine are the illustrations, which are for the most part reproductions from photo- graphs. There is hardly a place of interest in England or Wales for which a guide has not been provided, besides a guide for the Isle of Man. Wales and England, north, west, east, and south, are equally well covered. There are altogether no less than 23 of these penny guides. Just now the works of the late Mr. Edwin Waugh are in special demand. Mr. John Heywood has sent us copies of issues that he has in stock, and they are as follows :—" Th' barrel organ," "Snowed Up," " Owd Buzzart," " Owd Bodall," "Craig Dhu," "Chips," " Midgeclippings," " Comin' Whoam," and "Told by th' Winter Fire."

div.head: NE ‘l7. BOOKS,
div.p: NE ‘l7. BOOKS,

" y nil's Mystery" is the title of a new novel by Mr. Gorge Manville Fenn, published at 25., by Messrs. F. Warne and Co. It is hardly necessary to I say that, coming from this eminent popular author, the story is one which preserves the interest of the reader from beginning to end. It is a tale of murder and mystery, the details of the plot being admirably worked out. Mr. Fenn shows his skill in what he omits as well as what he states, and the result is that whatever criticism may be bestowed upon his work it can never be said that it is dull or tiresome. Messrs. Warne and Co. continue to issue children's books of a highly finished kind. We have to hand " Old Mother's Goose's Rhymes and Tales" (price is. 6d.), cleverly illustrated by Constance Haziewood. The illus- trations are numerous, and brilliant in colour, and vet it cannot be said that they are at all ton showy, the draw- ings being careful and the colours most harmonious. "The Marsh King's Daughter" is the title of one of Warne and Co's publications. The illustrations in Vas case are furnished by Jessie Currie. The drawings are large in size, and altogether striking. The price is is. "Texts for Illuminating" (price 6d.), contains twelve original outlines for handpainting, by Constance Hazle- wood. Directions and hints, with list of colours, are given, and there is a miniature example in each case which may be used as a guide in following up the out- lines. In the "Great Writers' Series," published by Mr. Walter Scott, we have to hand the life of Robert Brown- ing, by Mr. Wm. Sharp. This shilling life of the great poet, who has just left us, ought to prove exceedingly popular. It is the only full and authentic life of Brown- ing which has been issued, and it is due to Mr. Sharp to say, that it is written in a broad and yet critical spirit. The reader who is not familar with the works of Brown- ing will find the observations of Mr. Sharp both stimula- ting and helpful. So much has been said for and against Browning as a poet, that a work of this kind cannot fail to be useful in doing something like justice to a truly great writer. A passage from one of Browning's poems is quoted, which may be particularly used as applying to the poet himself. It runs as follows : One who never turned his back but marched breatt forward, Never doubted clouds would break; Never dreamed, though right were worsted, wrong would

_ triumph; Held we fall to rise, are baffled to fight better, Sleep to wake. Messrs. Cassell and Co. have just commenced the issue, in monthly parts, price 6d., of a very valuable work with the title of the "Dictionary of Religion." It is an ency- clopedia of Christian and other religious doctrines, denominations, sects, heresies, eccesiastical terms, &c. It is edited by the Rev. Dr. Benham, F.S.A. Along with the first part there is presented a map of the world, showing the distribution of religious, different colours being used to indicate the places which are Christian, Mahornmedan, or Bhuddist. "The Magazine of Art" for May has for frontispiece a beautiful photogravure of Mr. Herkomer's picture of the "Charterhouse. Mr. M. 11. Speilmann contributes an illustrated article on the Royal Academy, and Mr. W. M. Rosetti furnishes a second illustrated paper on the por- traits of Robert Browning. There are swne clever Rhone sketches by Mr. Joseph Pennell, and other illustrated articles are "Satsuma ware and its imitations," and "The Irish National Gallery." In the "Woman's World" the first article is devoted to "Mrs. Arthur Stannard at Home," with a portrait of the authoress and a view of her study. Otherillustrated papers are "Over Dutch Waterways," " Silk weaving in the East End," and "How to make fancy sleeves." There is, besides, the usual supply of fashion plates, and illustrations. Some of them are, this month, scarcely equal to the average. The contents of the current issue of "The Cabinet Portrait Gallery," are photographs of Dr. Allon, the Princesses Maud and Victoria of Wales, and Sir Frederick Abel. We have previously had to speak in terms of high praise of these charming photographs of Messrs. W. and D. Downey, and have onlyto repeat that there is no falling off in the wonderful quality of the work. The portraits of the two Princesses are perfect specimens of the photographic art. In part 4 of "Science for all," issued by Messrs. Cas- sell, the subjects dealt with are—" How plants feed," "Sleep," "Hills, dales, and valleys," "The sounds we hear," &c. We also have to hand from Messrs. Cassell the current issues of the "Dore Gallery," "Illustrated Shakes- peare," "Familiar Wild Flowers," "The Story of the Heavens," "The Sea," and "The World of Adven- ture." In " Cassell's Magazine" for May "The Stronger Will," and ". To be given up" are continued, whilst among the miscellaneous illustrated papers we Nave "How sounds are made Visible," "The American Par- liament," "A May Garden," "Robes of State," "Monograms." &c. In the " Quiver " the serial stories are—" In the Second Place," and "Worthy to be Loved." Part first is also Oven of a story by the Rev. P. B. Power, entitled "The Dreams of Dr. Faychng." Among other contents we have papers on "Revelations of Character," "Rest- lessness." "The Modern Sunday School," "Manifesta- tions of Christ," "Short Arrows," "Master Rockafellar's Voyage," and "Nobody's House," continue to delight the little ones who read "Little Folks." The serial contains, as usual, bright, readable sketches, all admirably illustrated. A The May Day number of the "Ladies Gazette of

div.head: MURDER OF A YOUNG WOMAN AND
div.p: MURDER OF A YOUNG WOMAN AND
ATTEMPTED SUICIDE.

------- -- Richard George Harding, aged 28, a builder, is in cus- tody at 'Kentish Town, on the chatge of murder. On Wednesday he went to the Victoria Tavern, in Clarence- road, and asked Mrs. Varney, the daughter of the pro- prietor, to take a stroll with him. She refused, wishing to have no further acquaintance with the young man. "If ,you don't come out, I will shoot you and myself, too,' Harding retorted, and he fired twice at the woman, bitting her in the neck. She fell dead. Harding then pointed the revolver at his own head and fired, but only damaged his hat rim. He afterwards made his way to a police station and confessed that he had shot the woman, saying he did not care what happened to him- self, but he felt sorry for his " old ,people.

LABOUR AND CAPITAL. THE EIGHT HOURS MOVEMENT. An open-air demoiastration attended by 20,000 persons was held in Aberdeen on Saturday afternoon. A resolu- tion was adopted at three platforms, calling for the institution of an eight hours working day. WAGES OF LANCASHIRE COTTON OPERATIVES. At the annual meeting of the Northern Counties Weavers' Association, representing 70,000 operatives, held on Saturday, at Burnley, it was resolved to give the employers of weaving. centres 14 days' notice to consider the adoption of a uniform wage list, and that unless they adopt Egtch a list the association would take the matter into its own hands.
