_ The Amalgamated Society of Salt and Alkali Workers, Northwich, recently sent a series of demands to the Salt Union for increase of pay and removal of grievances. The demands have been considered by the directors, and a few concessions made, but in most instances the pro- posals have been rejected. The men have requested an interview with the directors, which will shortly take place. THE FARM LABOURERS' AGUATION IN ANGLESEY. _ _

_ The reque,st made by the farm labourers, of Anglesey for a reduction of their hours of labour from 14 to 12 a day is generally being acceded to by the farmers. The hiring season for the summer term is now on, and the men hire to work from six a.m. to sig p.m. with very few exceptiohs. The demand of the labourers for a meal between dinner and six p.m. has been abandoned for the present.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
CRICKET.

At Westbury, on Saturday, the Colonial cricketers met with their first reverse, the match with Mr. Laverton's Eleven ending in favour of the Englishmen by 181 runs. After the rain on Friday evening the Australians had very little prospect of avoiding defeat, and the slight chance was completely destroyed (as that of the Englishmen at Sheffield Park had been on the previous Saturday) by the bright sunshine. When rain stopped play on Friday, Mr. Laverton's Eleven, who possessed a lead of 74 runs on the first innings, had at their second attempt put together 203 runs for the loss of seven wickets, so that in the most favourable conditions of weather and wicket the visitors would have had hard work to get the runs. Twenty minutes' play sufficed to bring the Englishmen's innings to a close for the addition of 20 runs, and with nearly four and a half hours left for play, and 298, runs set them. to win, the Australians went in to bat at a quarter to one. At lunch time they had lost half their wickets for 38. There were six men out for 43;. but Turner and Gregory stayed together for an hour, and added 53 runs. Turner, who went in fifth wicket down, was out ninth, at 109, having during the seventy-five minutes he was at the wickets batted in nice free style; for 47, which in- cluded four fours, three threes, and four twos. In the course of the match Ferris took twelve wickets for 125 runs, Briggs eleven for 92, and Lohmann seven for 77.

The rivalry of some years standing between the Earlestown and Golborne Cricket Clubs occasions almost as much interest in cricketing circles as the "ani- mosities" betwee the footballers of the respective places used to do in former times. The first match of the sea- son between the two teams took place at Golborne last Saturday and—well, the homesters did not win. The wazonmakers ran up 66 in good style while the decep- tive deliveries of Barker (Earlestown) played havoc with the Golborne stumps to the extent of 9 wickets for 14 runs. If he is a Barker he can also bite with a dogged determination.

The St. Helens Recreation Cricket Club seem to have made a splendid catch in Walter Robinson, the ex- Lancashire County man. Walter's cricketing days are far, very far, from being over, and this assertion will he supported by any spectator of his recent prowess in the field. Both in batting, bowling and fielding Robinson has fully justified the hopes entertained by the Recrea- tion Club in engaging his services.

In the match North v. South, a magnificent display of batting by Mr. Stoddart and some very fine bowling by Geo. Lohmann combined to gain for the South at Lord's an easy victory by 135 runs. The victorious side had much the best of the wicket, which was far easier before lunch than afterwards ; but as to the exceptional merit of what was done by the two cricketers named there can- not be any question. Mr. Stoddart opened the second innings of the South in company with Mr. Grace at a quarter to twelve and was the fifth man out, the total when he left being 169, out of which number he made no fewer than Ll 5! the result of two hours and 20 mine. cricket. He hit eighteen fours, four threes, and twelve twos, and at one point of his innings punished Ulyett for four hours from successive balls. Mr. Grace only made 29, but he was in with Mr. Stoddart while 111 runs were scored for the first wicket, the partnership lasting an hour and a half. The North wanted 245 to win—a tremendous task under the circumstances—and seven wickets were down for 58. Shrewsbury, who again played very finely, was out at 78, but Mr. Hornby and Attewell gave some trouble before the end came, exactly at half past six. Lohmann took eight wickets, seven of them bowled down, at a cost of 65 runs, and against such a team this was a great performance.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

The members of the Warrington Chests Club have been busy lately, having met in friendly encounter representa- tives. of Wigan and Widnes. In both their meetings Wigan proved the stronger team, though in their return match the Warringtonians were only a point or two behind. Widnes, however, had to succumb in both matches played to the superior prowess of the local club, which although quite a young institution is full of vigour.

Warrington athletes were to the front at some of the gatherings on Saturday. In the 120 yards handicap flat race, at the amoral meeting of the Manchester Athletic Club, J. Worrall, of Warrington,succeedeci in carrying off the second prize, and at the Oldham Sports, J. Massey ran in second in the 220 yards maiden handicap. In the two miles inter-club steeplechase, the Warrington Harriers were successful in obtaining the second position. The local representatives came in in the following order: —J. Massey, 3rd ; J. Barlow, 13th ; and W. Price, 12th ; total, 23. The winners' (Salford Harriers) representa- tives ran in grand style, and obtained the first, second, and fourth places.

div.head: lab' LICE TRAGEDY.
div.p: lab' LICE TRAGEDY.

TRIAL A.ND VERDICT. The trial of William. Dickinson,. 22, a collier of Ice, near Wigan and Ann Die Wilson, his wife, on a charge of having murdered Hannah Lydia Bircholl,, aged 6, the daughter of the female prisoner by a former husband, has occupied the attention of Baron Fluddlerston and the jury at the Liverpool Assizes, since Friday last.—Mr. McConnell and Mr. Collingwood Elope, prosecuted; Mr. Shee and Mr. Hugh Fort defended..—At the request of the counsel the judge decided to.try the prisoners sepa- rately, the case against the male prisoner being first opened, The murder was one of peculiar atrocity. On the night in question the mother went out, leaving the deceased,.who was described as an attractive child, at home with the male prisoner. When she returned the child was missing, and no trace of her could be dis- covered. Some days afterwards the body was discovered in a disused pit shaft leading to what is known as the Ravine Mine, near the prisoner's house,and on examina- tion it was found that the child had been outraged. It was stated that the female prisoner had been seen wash- ing blood-stains clut of clothing worn by the male prisoner. The depositions of John Hennessey, the owner of the Ravine Mine, who had died since the 9th March, were put in. Hennessey had stated before the magis- trates that on the afternoon of the sth March the mouth of the pit was secure, and on the following day he met the prisoner about the place. On that day witness also saw that a quantity of the slag had been removed from the pit's mouth. Peter Dickinson brother of the prisoner, in his evidence said that he had found some hairs very like those of the deceased on some of the old iron at , the mouth of the pit. This led to a man named Orrell going down the pit, and at the bottom, lying on some debris, he found the dead body of the child. Several witnesses admitted that the prisoner seemed anxious to find the girl when his neighbours were making a search for her.—James Orrell said he volunteered to go down the mine in search of the girk When he found the body at the bottom of the pit, it was minus a hat, dress, and clogs. There was no blood about the bottom of the mine near the body, and there were no streaks or spots of Wood on her clothing.— The brother of the prisoner said that the deceased was an illegitimate child.—Mr. Shee said that he had several witnesses to call for the defence. Amongst others he called Dr. Berry, who said he examined the prisoner, and found two or three cuts on his left hand. The stains on his trousers pocket, his shirt, and his handker- chief were such as might have been caused by a bleeding finger, and the marks on the quilt were consistent with what might happen at a confinement. He did not think that the injuries to the girl could have been caused by a man, but they might bee. the result of a fall down a pit. Bearing in mind that water was constantly falling down the pit, any blood which flowed from the injuries would become diluted and in a few days would not easily be discovered.—Dr. W. G. Barnish, Medical Officer of Health for Wigan, gave corroborative evidence. On Tuesday Baron Huddleston proceeded to sum up the case.—Afterone hour's deliberation the jury found a verdict of "Not guilty." Mr. McConnell said on behalf of the prosecution he would now offer no evidefice against Ann Dickinson. He had resolved upon this course before the verdict of the jury was given in the case against the man, and his decision was, of course, kreatly strengthened by the verdict.—By the direction of his lordship, the jury acquitted thewoman.—The judge: Let both prisoners be discharged.—Subsequently, the jury handed to his lordship a rider to their verdict, to the effect, that they were of opinion that a most atro- cious murder had been committed, but there was not sufficient evidence to show by whom.—The man Dickin- son was mobbed as he left the court. He was recog- nised by the crowd and followed, hooted at, and threat- ened with violence. He took refuge in a public-house, telling the barmaid he thought the crowd would kill him. The police had to clear the house, and Dickinson was ultimately got away through a back door, and into a cab, in which he drove off. After his discharge at the Liverpool Assizes, on Tues- day, Dickinson and his wife arrived in St. Helens between four and five o'clock. It is stated that they proceeded to the house of a relative in the Denton's-green district. During the evening he called at the Ilesketh Arms, in Church-st., with a friend, and had a glass of beer, but he only stayed in the back room for a minute or two, and scarcely uttered a word. He was not known, and accordingly no curiosity or interest was manifested. William Dickinson has returned to Ince. On Thursday morning he accompanied his brother to work at the Bottom Place colliery. The excitement of the first few days has toned down, and people have assumed a more friendly attitude towards him. He and his wife returned late in the evening, and were, therefore left to 'go their way unmolested.

div.head: ARE MOST MEN HONEST?
div.p: ARE MOST MEN HONEST?

Are the majority of men honest or dishonest? A deep and difficult question. A famous king said, "All men are liars." Was he right? Can we trust one another? Is every second man you meet a thief ?—either in fact or at heart? Are most men governed by conscience and a sense of honour? As we decide this point, so must we treat our fellows in our dealings with them. The follow- ing story will throw light upon this question: Some years ago an American business man had an article to sell which he believed would prove popular and useful in Great Britain, if he could introduce it here. He came to England without an introduction, without friends in this country, and with very little money, yet he felt at once a strange confidence and astrangediffidence. His diffidence arose from his being a stranger in a strange land, and that the people might imagine that the article he desired to sell was of no value, and merely intended to deceive the purchaser. His confidence was based upon his know- ledge of the rectitude of his own intentions, and that the public would approve what he proposed to supply them with as soon as they became acquainted with it. Buthow should he induce them to test it? That was the perplexing problem in his mind. He solved this problem in a manner we may properly call original, and which at first appeared the very height of folly. He took the ground that the great majority of people will prove honest if you trust them. bn this theory he acted. He placed his goods, to the value a( thousands of pounds, in the hands of utter strangers, trusting to their word of honour alone that if they sold them they would pay for them. This he did all over the country. The business men of Londhn, where he began his operations, heard of this with amazement. They called him an idiot and a lunatic, and predicted that he would be .robbed and cheated right and left. But the result proved that our American friend was right, and all his critics wrong. The public soon found the goods were exactly what they were represented to be; they bought eagerly, and every shilling due was remitted without hesitation or difficulty, and a trade sprang up which in a few years caused him to rank as one of the most successful men in his line of business in the world. Ile had demonstrated that the great majority of people are honest, and considered the experience of incalculable value. He trusted the English public and trusts them constantly, with the same results. We may state, as the matter is now no secret, that the man was Mr. A. .1. White, and the article he had to sell was Mother SeigePs Curative Syrup, a medicine the name of which is to-day a household word all over the civilised earth. This preparation, the con- stituents of which were discovered by the old German nurse whose name it bears, is now everywhere conceded to be an infallible remedy tor constipation, indigestion, dyspepsia, and all ailments arising from an impare state of the blood. Its great fame has not grown out of extensive and cunning advertising, but from de mouth to mouth and door to door comments and praises of the people themselves. All who use it are cured; then they tell the news to their neighbours, and so it flies from town to town and from land to land.

_ Everybody is supposed to know the symptoms of in- digestion and dyspepsia, yet it will do no harm to name the principal ones again, especially for the reason that it is often mistaken for other diseases,, to the loss of time and money : Frequent or continual headache ; a dull pain at the base of the brain; bad breath ; nauseous eructa- tions ; the rising of sour and pungent fluids totlae throat a sense of oppression and faintness at the pit of the stomach ; flatulence ; wakefulnes% and loss of sleep; dis- gust with food even when weak from the need of it; sticky or slimy matter on the teeth or in the mouth, especially on rising in the m orning ; furred and coated tongue ; dull eyes; cold hands and feet ; constipation; dry or rough skin; inability to fix the mind on any labour calling for continuous attention; and oppressive and sad forebodings. When you feel any of these syrup- terns—and they comprise nirke-tenths of our ailments— Seigers Syrup is as certain to relieve and cure you as you are to take it. An army of people have testified to this over their own signatures, and a still greater host, averse to having their names in print have privately given the facts and their names for confidential use. We may, therefore, say that Mr. White has demons- trated two things by his odd experiment—the honesty of the people and the honesty of what he had to sell them.

div.head: MURDER OF AN AI7NT.
div.p: THE MURDER OF AN AI7NT.

Alfred Eastwell was charged on remand at Lambeth Police Court, on Saturday, with the wilful murder of Theresa Heizenbuzzle, his aunt, by shooting her. Dr. Gallie said the prisoner when arrested was suffering from delirium tremens. The priscner was committed for trial.

div.head: GUNPOWDER EXPLOSION.
div.p: THE GUNPOWDER EXPLOSION.
34 BODIES RECOVERED.

Further intelligence from Havana shows that the explosion on Saturday was even more disastrous than was at first believed. Thirty-four bodies have now been recovered, and it is feared others still lie buried beneath the debris. The theatres are temporarily closed. The Chamber of Commerce and other public bodies have sus- pended the sittings. Flags are flying half-mast, and other signs of mourning are everywhere visible. The proprietor of the store where the e_xplosion occurred has been arrested. a

div.head: POLITICAL.
div.p: POLITICAL.

Mr. F. W. Maude, who was formerly secretary of the Liberal Unionist Association, will be the Glacistonian Liberal candidate for East Dorset. At the annual meeting of the Keighley County Liberal Association, held on Saturday, Mr. Isaac Holden M.P.. was adopted as the Liberal candidate for the division at the next election. The Liberal Unionist Association of St. Rollox Division of Glasgow have called upon Professor Caldwell to resign the office of honorary president, and instructed the executive to select another Unionist_candidate. _ _ _ .

-. Through Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P., the Carnarvon Liberal Association have received permission to organize an excursion to Rawarden on Whit-Thursday. It is in- tended to present Mr. Gladstone with addresses from the Carnarvon Reform Club and the Ladies' Liberal League.

div.head: MR. CHAMBERLAIN AGAIN.
div.p: MR. CHAMBERLAIN AGAIN.

Speaking on Monday night to the Liberal Unionists of Birmingham, Mr. J. Chamberlain, M.P., asserted that the Liberals could not define Home Rule because it had not been defined for them by their leader. After stating that if the Liberal party styled themselves the party of promise he was ready to admit their claim, he referred to Mr. Gladstone's progress through East Angfia, criticised the conduct of the Opposition, and said that the Licensing Bill of the Government was an honest attempt to pro- mote temperance, and it ought not to be treated with scorn and suspicion.

IN our last issue we pointed out The Bridges that the Manchester Ship Canal Question. Company had not applied for authority under their new bill to abandon Ackers- lane swing-bridge, and that this might prove a fa- tal objection to their attempt to deprive the inha- bitants of Latchford of one means of crossing the canal. But the plot develops quickly ; the Com- pany are now seeking to remedy this defect by a special application to Parliament; and everything would seem to be cut and dried for rushing the new clauses through, and riding rough-shod over the bulk of the residents. We say the bulk, be- because it is notorious that Ackers-lane bridge is to be sacrificed—if the Company can have their way—in order that a few carriage people may be accommodated, at another point, with a high-level vehicular bridge. It comes to this that two swing bridges on two important roads—Grappenhall-road and Ackers-lane—are to be given up for one high-level bridge which is to be placed where, at present, there is no road at all. It is true that it is proposed to make a road, and that it will terminate at one end at the gate of Mr. JOHN WHITE'S house, who is a strong advo- cate of this scheme for sacrificing the masses to the classes. It is true, too, that Mr. JOHN WHITE is agent for Sir GILBERT GREENALL, and that, con- current with the abandonment of Ackers-lane swing bridge, the Ship Canal Company are re- quired to make a road which will run along the south bank of the Ship Canal to Stockton Heath— a road whkh will be of little use to the people liv- ing on the north side of the Canal ; but which will have the saving merit of opening out the land belonging to Messrs. GREENALL, WHITLEY, AND CO. This is another glaring instance of the way in which private interests aro served whilst public interests are sacrificed.

The organ which Mr. Joini. WHITE is understood to inspire sneers at the Rev. F. L. GOOD for re- ferring to the inconvenience which people trudging on foot would be put to in getting over a bridge which will be at least double the height of the bridge at Wilderspool crossing But the argu- ment remains, and the people remain, despite the sneer, and, if the authorities who have been ap- pealed to do their duty, the needs of the many will not be set aside to gratify the whims of the few. The only thing that has been urged in favour of the high-level carriage bridge is that it will enable people to cross the Ship Canal without at any time having to run the risk of waiting whilst a ship goes by. But the Canal Company met this objec- tion by undertaking to provide a foot bridge, on condition that Grappenhall-road swing bridge should be abandoned. This was agreed to; the new bill was drawn upon this understanding, and now, at the eleventh hour, a score or so of carriage people step in and say :--" We cannot use this foot-bridge; and we won't risk being detained at a ' swing bridge. The Canal Company must convert the foot-bridge, for our especial conveni- ence, into a carriage-road, and we will sacrifice Ackers-lane bridge as well as Grappenhall-roa d bridge." It is nothing to the purpose that

swing bridge is to be used over Knutsford-readf and over every other main road. These great ones of Grappenhall must have a bridge to themselves, whoever may suffer. It will suit the Canal Com- pany,of course, tohave to make one bridge instead. . of two ; for it will save them many thousands of : pounds. • But the arrangement (7.oes not suit the ipublic, .and if the members of . the Cheshire' County Council, the Daresbury Highway Board,. and the Warrington Corporation do their duty it . will not become law ; it will be opposed and.. rejected by Parliament. .

We are not afraid of England being delivered oveF .. to "Rome Rule," especially since the Nationaliste. of Ireland have made it clear that they do ncl take their politics from the Vatican; but all the. same we desire to see something like consisteneY . in our dealings with Rome, and wish to Im..er.- . exactly whither we are are going. If the Court of Rome is to permitted to determine the validity of a marriage . between a Catholic and a non-Catholic M why not in Ireland or in England ? it may a small issue on the face of it, but in so far involves a principle it may come to be a large .. issue. We should certainly like to be something more of this new departure before git" , . ing even a qualified assent to it. The Papal Coal.' has its place and its functions; and due regeru` should be paid to those functions; but they ought .' not to over-ride English law and English custom ill controlling English subjects—whether they re- side in Malta or Manitoba. In the case in question, George, Crawford, landlord of the "Old House at Here, was summoned for permitting drunkenness on premises, and Henry Morris and Mary Mogi!, were summoned for having been drunk on the sai" premises. Police Sergeant Cheney and Police Constables Barnett and Corbett severally testifiea to the Morrises being found drunk and drinking the "Old House at Home." div.p: STRIKE AT WIDNES.
Yesterday, the "Salt Cake" men, labourers employed in the manufacture of salt cake at Widnes, struck work for an advance of 3d. a ton. Nearly 1,000 men arc affected.
POOR RATES IN WIDNES DISTRICT.

At the Widnes Petty Sessions,on Thursday, the magis- trates sanctioned the laying of the following poor rates For the toWnship of Widnes, at 2s. in the £ ; Ditton, is. in the R ; Cronton, Is. in the £ ; and Bold, Is. in the R. BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH RUNCORN.

To-morrow morning, in this place of warship, the Rev. John Simpson, the newly appointed pastor, will conduct a children's service, and at the evening service the rev, gentleman will preach a sermon on " The Mystery of Temptation."

div.head: RUNCORN FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY.
div.p: RUNCORN FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY.

At the last meeting of the Committee the Librarian reported that during April 2,240 books had been issued from the Library, a decrease of nine. It was resolved to close the Library on Whit Tuesday, but to open the read- ing room as usual.

div.p: Sr. PAUL'S CHAPEL, RUNCOHN..

_ The choir anniversary in connection with this Chapel will be held to-morrow, when the Rev. J. Judson will preach in the morning, and the Rev. H. Burson in the evening. The Choi: YMlrriqer specially s.elected chants and anthems at each service. SUMMER FasutoNs now showing at W. BUTTON'S, Sankey-Bf., Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: SUSPICIOUS CHARACTERS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: SUSPICIOUS CHARACTERS AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, before Mr. G. L.pavies, Michael Gorman and John Riley,strangers, were charged with frequentinv Wellington-st. with in- tent to commit a felony. The -prisoners, on the previous morning, were seen by Detective Woodrow, acting in a suspicious manner. While one went into the shops and public-houses, the other kept watch outside, and the officer afterwards learned that no purchases had been made. lie therefore apprehended them on suspicion.— The prisoners were discharged on promising to leave the town.

WIDNES COUNTY COURT. At this court yesterday, before His Honour Judge Goldthorpe, an action was brought by Yates Brothers, grocers, of Widnes-road, to recover £ll. 9s. 6d. for damages to a trap caused by a traction engine belonging to Messrs. Short. Mr. J. W. Knowles was for the com- plainant, and Mr. C.H. Lewin for the detendant. It was alleged that whilst going along the road at Lunt's Heath, the engine ran into the trap and did the damage stated. The evidence for the defence was that the trap ran into the engine. His Honour gave a verdict for the defendant.
SUMMER FASHIONS now showing at J. &W. DyTToti's Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. FOUND DEAD IN THE MERSEY AT RUNCORN.

On Thursday, at the Cemetery Office, Runcorn, Mr J. E. Worsley, the coroner, held an inquest on the body of a man unknown, which was found on the " gridiron" at the end of No Man's Land, on Tuesday evening, by P. Stubbs. P.C. Crowder deposed that the body was in a highly decomposed state and was evidently that of a sailor between 45 and 50 years of age. He had not been identified. His wearing apparel consisted of moleskin trousers, blue worsted guernsey,blue check shirt, lace-up boots and blue stockings. The deceased bad no beard or moustache.—A verdict of "found dead was recorded.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH AT RUNCORN.
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH AT RUNCORN.

Mr. J. E. Worsley, the coroner, held an inquest at the Cemetery Office, Runcorn, on Thursday afternoon, into the circumstances of the death of John Ford, 57 years of age, a dock porter' who had lived at Doyle's Lodging- house in Mersey-A. The deceased had been out of work for several weeks through illness, and not having money to pay for his lodgings, went to his son's house on Satur- day. He complained of a lump at his heart,and had had medicine from Dr. Mangan and " Sequah," but nothing, he said, seemed to do him good. On Tuesday morning his daughter-in-law found him dead in bed.—Dr. Mangan said he had made a post-mortem and death was the result of valvular disease of the heart. The jury returned a verdict accordingly. TRAVELLING TRUNKS.—Garland, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge- d.. Warrington.

div.head: WOUNDING A WIDNES PUBLICAN.
div.p: WOUNDING A WIDNES PUBLICAN.

On Wednesday, at Widnes Police Court, John Crinow, a powerfully built young man, was charged with unlaw- fully womading Joseph Dixon landlord of the Swan Inn, Waterloo-rd. About nine o'clock on Monday night, the prisoner went into Mr. Dixon's house, and asked a ques- tion. On being answered he left the premises, and in .a few minutes a brick was thrown through one of the glass doors at the entrance to the bar. Mr. Dixon went out- side, and seeing the prisoner running away, went in pursuit. The prisoner turned 'round and threw a stone at his pursuer, who was struck on the forehead and seriously injured. Subsequently the wound was stitched and dressed by Dr. Hutchinson,and the prisoner was given into custody. The magistrate committed the prisoner to the Quarter Sessions for trial. UNNAPIIY MARRILD LIFE AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, John Kaye, of Witt-rd., was summoned for refusing to contribute to- wards his wife's maintenanoe. Mr. J. W. Knowles appeared for the complainant, and Mr. Swift for the defendant.--Mr. Knowles said the complainant applied for a maintenance order under the Act of 1886. The parties were married on the 7th October, 1887, and for 18 months lived comfortably together.—The wife, Sarah Jane Kaye, was called, and said she was willing to live with the defendant.—Mr. Swift: The defendant does not see his way to go back to her after what has occurred.— The defendant said his earnings were £l4s. 10d. a week, and the Bench considered the desertion proved, and ordered the defendant to pay 6s. per week towards his wife's support. SUMMER FASHIONS. TIOW showing at J. &W. DUTTON'S, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Adet.

div.head: WIDNES DOCTRESS AND HER PRESCRIPTIONS.
div.p: A WIDNES DOCTRESS AND HER PRESCRIPTIONS.

Elizabeth Welsh, of West Bank, was summoned before the Widnes magistrates on Thursday charged with ssaulting Elizabeth Hislop on the 10th inst. It was alleged that as the complainant was passing the defend- ant's house the latter called her in to "have a quiet talk," and tken struck her on the temple and the back of the head. The complainant ran into an adjoining house, where the defendant followed and again assaulted her, knocking a tooth out.— In cross-examination by Mr. Knowles, the complainant said she was a doctress, but had given up the business Weans° it did not pay. She had a book of prescriptions worth £l,OOO. She denied that she had made the defendant's children afraid by her superstitious nonsense.—Mr. Knowles said the complain- ant was the humbug of the neighbourhood; she pre- tended that she was a relation of the Queen, and that Lady Stapleton was her aunt and Godmother.—After hearing the evidgpce, the Bench found that an assault had been committed, and fined the defendant ss. and costs. _

div.head: MISTAKEN TRAVELLERS AT WIDNES.
div.p: MISTAKEN TRAVELLERS AT WIDNES.

At the i'Vkin-e-s-'Po-lic—e Court, on Monday, before Messrs. G. Pilkington and H. Gaskell, junior, Benjamin Bell, Hughes-street, and Robert Notman Grenfell-street, Widnes, were each summoned for falsely representing themselves as travellers at Bold on the 4th inst.—P.C. Foster stated that at half-past eleven on Sunday, the 4th inst.' he saw the two defendants go into the beerhouse of Elizabeth Heyes, at Bold. Witness, in company with Sergt. Cracken, followed them, and found they had been sup- plied with a pint of beer each. They both lived within the distance of three miles and were not entitled to be served with beer.—Eliza Winstanley sari she assisted Mrs. Hayes in conducting her beerhouse. On the day in question the defendants came to the back door,and asked Mrs. Heyes if there was any chance of getting a drink. They said they had come from the" Snig "—rhe consta- ble (recalled) said both defendants lived at Simm's Cross, Widnes. Notman said they thought they were fully three miles from Widnes.—Both cases were dismissed on the defendants agreeing to pay the costs. GARDEN TOOLS.—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger, Warrington & Earlestown.

div.head: WILL OF SIR T. EDWARDS-MOSS, BART.
div.p: WILL OF SIR T. EDWARDS-MOSS, BART.

The will of the late Sir T,, Edwards-Moss, Bart., has been proved in the Liverpool Probate Registry, the net personalty being sworn at £494,844. The testator leaves certain legacies, including £lO,OOO to Mr. Zoro Innes, who was long engaged in Moss's Bank;" £5OO each to his brother, Mr. G. W. Moss, and Mrs. G. W. Moss; £5,000 each to his two daughters, Minna Amy and Mary Ethel ; £lOO to each of his grand-children and nephews; £lOO each to his butler and wife, and one year's wages to each of his servants who has been in his service upwards of five years. His two sons, Sir Jno. E. Edwards-Moss and Mr. Tom Cottingham Edward-Moss, are given the sum of £l,OOO to distribute for charitable and benevolent purposes as they think fit. The present baronet obtains the tenancy for life of the estate at Otterspool, and here- ditaments in Toxteth-park, &c., together with the furni, ture, books, and carriages at Otterspool. A portion of the plate is, however, left to Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss, and the jewellery to the testator's daughters. In addition to the Otterspool estate, Sir Jno. E. Edwards-Moss is bequeathed the sum of £250,000. Mr. T. E. Edwards-Moss receives £lOO,OOO, together with all the testator's estates in British Guiana and South America, whilst the residue of the per- sonalty, together with reversionary interest, estimated at £250,000, is to be held in trust to be invested- in real estate in England and Wales. Such properties the testa- tor directs to be entailed, gild to pass to his heirs in order of primogeniture.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 24, 1890
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 24, 1890
RUNCORN VOLUNTEERS ON PARADE.

A church parade of the Runcorn Companies of the 2nd Battalion, Cheshire Regiment, took place on Sunday, when about 80 members of the corps, with Lieutenant Lightburn, marched to Trinity Church under the com- mand of Captain Wigg. An appropriate sermon was ureached by the Rev. Dr. Preston, chaplain. To-day (Saturday) the regiment depart for Conway, to spend a week under canvas.

div.head: DROWNINGMYSTRRIRS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: DROWNINGMYSTRRIRS AT RUNCORN.

An inquest was held at the Burial Board Office, on Mon- day, by Mr. J. E. Worslev, respecting the death of John' Popplewell, a boatman, whose body was found in a lock on the Bridgewater Canal, at Runcorn, on Friday night. On Thursday night a man named Wm. Beech, met the deceased, who said he was starved and desired to sell his shirt. At that time he said he was going to sleep on a boat ; and nothing snore was heard of him. As there was mo evidence to show how the deceased got into the water, a verdict of "Found drowned" was returned. On Tuesday afternoon' Mr. Worsley held an inquest at Wes- ton Point on the body of a youth, named Arthur Robin- son aged 16 years, who was employed at the Weston Point Salt Works. On Sunday morning Robinson was seen sculling a boat in the Dock of the Works, and subse- quently he was missed. On Monday morning the dock was dragged and his dead body found. A verdict of "Found drowned" was returned.
RUNCORN AND DISTRICT PEERS ECONOMIC BUILDING SOCIETY.

The first annual nieeting was held in Bethesda Lecture Hall on Friday night last. Mr. J. J. Speakman presided In their report the directors congratulate the members on the success achieved. Although the profit and loss account showed an apparent loss of £26 10s., it should be taken into consideration that all books, forms, prelim- inary and working- expenses had been paid, and the society was now clear of all these liabilities. In addi- tion the society had two appropriations of £2OO each in hand, the profit on which when sold would probably realise £BO. The sale of these is, however, held in abey- ance for the present, in order to give members a prefer- ence should they win a ballot. The society consists of 165 members hold.ng 330 shares and the income from sub- scriptions amounts to £339 14s. The members were urged to do all in their power to bring the membership up to the maximum number.—On the proposition of the Chairman the report and balance sheet were adopted. SIINI7vIEn FASHIONS, now showing at T. & W, Burros's, 6ankey-st., Warriogtont-444, NiitftOw IsdAP26 Olst THE WEAVRE. A small steamer known as the Chanticleer, plying on the river Weaver, got her prow under a bar in the Vale Royal Loch on Wednesday, and when the water rushed into the 102 h the boat filled and sank. Enoch Houlgrave, the engineer, was in the engine- room at the time, and had a very narrow escape, making his way on deck with difficulty, and being rescued just as the boat went down.

div.head: _ A CHANCE FOR THE SHIP CANAL.
div.p: _ A CHANCE FOR THE SHIP CANAL.

At a meeting of the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, on Thursday a letter was read from Mr. T. H. Ismay, of the White Star Line, pointing out that the alterations resolved upon by the Board fell short of what was required to enable Liverpool to retain its hold upon the transatlantic trade. A large number of cargo steamers were capable of being loaded at a depth of 28ft. or more, yet there would only be 23ft. of water at the lowest spring tide. There should, he contended, also be a deeper dock sill. In view of the rapid strides in shipbuilding and the importance of the trade interests involved, he urged the Board to reconsider the matter.

div.head: NEWTON DIVISION .LIBERAL. AssocuioN..
div.p: NEWTON DIVISION .LIBERAL. AssocuioN..

A general meeting of the executive of the Newton Division Liberal Association was held on Tuesday evening, at the Earlestown and District Liberal Club, Fairclough-st., Earlestown. The chair was occupied by Mr. Geo. W. Rawlins C.C., and there was a good representative attendance. The pro- ceedings were of a private character. After the minutes of the last meeting had been read and confirmed we understand that matters affecting the position of the Liberal party in the division were discussed, and there was a general expression of opinion favourable to a more vigorous prosecution of political affairs in the district, from a Liberal standpoint. . _ _
SUMMER iesaroNs, now showing at J. & W. EtrrroN s, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. WEST LANCASHIRE RUGBY ALLIANCE.

A general meeting of the West Lancashire Rugby Alliance was held at the Fleece Hotel, St. Helens, on Saturday evening. Mr. F. T. Parry occupied the chair, and the following clubs were represented : High field, Standard South End,Sutton,Wigan Rovers, Thatto Heath, West Leigh, Widnes St. Mary's Run- corn Recreation, and Horwich. The meeting was specially called to arrange the Alliance fixtures for next season, the only clubs absent being Litherland and Frodsham. All dates were satisfactorily fixed, and the chairman announced that the annual general meeting of the Union will be held at Liverpool on Saturday the 31st inst. After some discussion re Alliance rules, a vote of thanks to the chairman closed the meeting.

A 'HOUSE STRUCK BY LIGHTNING AT ST. HELENS. Between one and two o'clock on Tuesday morning, a heavy thunderstorm passed over St. Helens and district. The lightning was of a vivid nature, the thunderclaps unusually startling, and rain fell in torrents. The storm reached its climax about half- past one when a brilliant flash of forked lightning descended right into tbe heart of the town, followed by a peal of thunder which awoke almost the entire town. A block of six houses, recently erected by Councillor Bennett in Ormskirk-st., was.struck and two sisters named Mary Winifred Cullen, aged twenty-two, and Annie Cullen, aged fifteen, had a narrow escape. They live with their mother, Mrs. Elizabeth Cullen. a carpetmaker, and were asleep in the front bedroom, when the chimney stack was struck by the electrie fluid. One side of it was torn away, and the debris fell upon the roof, and into the street and backyard. The current passed down* the chimneys, carrying soot and plaster into the rooms and damaging the walls and pictures. The bed was near to the fire-place and the wall was broken and burntiwithin a few inches of their heads, but with the exception of being covered with plaster, &c., the occupants were uninjured.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Present, Colonel Ashton, chairman, Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Mclntyre. J. Stokes, J. Weir, J. Baguley, P. Hall, T. Lewis, H. E. Heywood, John Bate, J. Brandreth, J. Smith, J. Whitlow, J. Parr, Hewitt,C. Philips, Bretherton, H. Linaker (clerk), H. G Linaker (assistant clerk).
SPECIAL PREC'EPT. S.

The assistant Clerk reported that precepts for special expenses be issu'ed as follows :—Appleton-with-Hull, £120; Frodsham £l7O, Frodsham Lordship £BO, and Helsby £3O. These, he said, required a special rate.— The necessary resolution was carried.

div.head: HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.
div.p: HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.

The Medical Officer reported two cases of diptheria at Halton and sanitary defects had been remedied. A case of typhoid fever had occurred at Dutton Workhouse, and another at Kinzswood. There was a further out- break of scarlatina at Netherton.

div.head: NUISANCE AT WESTON.
div.p: NUISANCE AT WESTON.

The Inspector of Nuisances reported that in accordance with instructions he had given notice tc open a sewer at Lambsickle-lane, Weston. The sewer was now tem- porarily open and there was no nuisance on the premises at present, but a nuisance would occur again unless the sewer were watched.

POLLUTION OF A BROOK. Mr. C. L. Evans, agent to the Norton Estate wrote complaining about the pollution of Keekwick Brook. From what he could learn the pollution arose from the Tannery at Preston Brook, discharging refuse water into it. It was a very serious detriment to the farms through which the brook flowed as naturally the farmers did not like their cattle to drink the water, as there was no doubt it must affect the milk. The authority instructed the inspector to inspect the course of the brook and report to the Clerk.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Wsilthouswon Tuesday. Colonel Ashton presided, and there were present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. H. J. (rice, P. Speakman, P. Hall, J. Weir, T. Lewis, J. Baguley, H. E. Hey- wood, J. W. Baguley, Priestner, W. Fisher, C. Phillips, Bretherton, Smith, Yarwood, J. Brandreth, J. Whitlow, Parr, S. Taylor, Mclntyre, Hewitt, H. Linaker (clerk), H. G. Linaker (deputy clerk.)

div.head: CHEQUE WANTED- .
div.p: A CHEQUE WANTED- .

Mr. Reginald Potts, clerk to Cheshire County Council wrote stating that the balance of the amount of the pre- cept for the county and police rates payable by the Run- corn Union, and which was made returnable on the first of March last, had not yet been received by the County Treasurer, and he should be obliged if they would for- ward a cheque for the amount with as little delay as possible. DESTITUTE GIRLS. . . - .

Maria Fryer of the emigration Home for Destitute Girls, London, wrote, asking whether the Guardians had any Protestant girls petween the age of -nine and 13 that *light be taken to Canada in August. The children must be in good health, and fair intelligence and the cost to the Guardians would be £8 each child; and a complete outfit, and must be handed °ger free at Liverpool.—Mr. Brandreth said the outfit would cost a further £6—Mr Griatif we wanted to send any out we should have to ask the consent of the relatives.—The Clerk replied that was so.—Mr. Speakman remarked that there were no such girls to spare out of the house. RAYING OF MACHINERY. On the proposition of Mr. Mclntyre, seconded by Mr. Speakmin, the seal of the Board was attached to a peti- tion to Parliament against the Rating of Machinery
(Exemption) Bill.—ln reply to Mr. Fisher, the Clerk said if the Bill were passed it would affect Runcorn Union to the extent of several thousands. The seal was affixed.
FINANCE.

_ Mr. Brundrit presented the report of the Finance Committee, who recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £2,773 17s. id. Of this amount £2,670 13s. sd. was the outstanding debt due to the County Council. Another item was £B6 18s. 2d. interest and repayment of loan on the workhouse. The loan on the House was now £1,659 7s. 10d. After these liabilities had been met there would be a small balance in the treasurer's hands.

div.head: WIDNES LIBERAL ASSOCIATION AND COMPENSATION.
div.p: WIDNES LIBERAL ASSOCIATION AND COMPENSATION.

The annual meeting in connection with Whines Division Liberal Association for the purpose of electing representatives to the General Council was held in the Widnes Liberal Club, on Monday night. Mr. E. Carey presided, and there was a moderate attendance. The Chairman, after explaining that Mr. Charles Crompton i Q.C., was unable to be pre- sent through illness, proposed "That this meeting desires to record its earnest protest against the Compensation or Endowment Clauses of the Local Taxation (Customs and Excise) Bill, for the follow- ing amongst other reasons: That the constituencies have not been consulted upon the subject, and that the tendency of the clauses is to create a vested interest where none has hitherto existed." Mr. Carey said they I were not merely opposing the giving of compensation to publicans who had been by the public vote deprived of their living and interest, but the form in which the com- pensation should be given. The form of compensation proposed by the Government would considerably increase in value the public-houses that remained, and create a vested interest which had not hitherto existed.—Mr. S. K. Muspratt seconded the upotion. The Compensation Clauses, he argued, were simply a bribe to all those voters who put the present Government in power. He thought the Constituences ought themselves to decide how many public-houses were necessary.—Mr. J. Morri- son, Mr. F. J. Poole, and Mr. F. Hartland supported the motion which was carried uaanhnously.—The business of the meeting was then transacted in the usual form.

div.head: RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB, ANNUAL IiEETING.
div.p: RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB, ANNUAL IiEETING.

The annual meeting of the members of the Run- corn Football Club was held in the large room at Mr. Riley's Café, on Tuesday evening. Mr. A. Jor- dan presided, and there was a capital attendance. The secretary (Mr. J. E. Laugshaw) read the report, which gave the statistics of the last season's matches, which appeared in this journal last week, with the exception of the goal-kicking averages, which showed that Crodipton had kicked 52 goals in 82 attempts ; J. Braze/Wale, 16 goals, 53 attempts ; S. , Houghton, 2 goals, 9 attempts ; and Woods, 3 goals, 6 attempts.—Mr. C. Pownalt (treasurer) presented the financial statement, which showed a balance in hand of £2l 4s. 2d.—The Chairman, in moving the adoption of the reports, referred with satisfaction to the fact that they had a balance in hand, although it was not a large one. As to the last season's work, there were few clubs in the country that could show such splendid results as the Runcorn Club ; and in analysing the reasons for that remarkable success they must give credit to each in- dividual member, for he was sure, that no impartial spectator could help seeing that every member, of both the first and second teams had played as if the games depended upon his individual effort. (Applause.) Another reason why the score stood so prominent ,was the style of play that had been developed by the Club. Wherever they went, they heard the spectators praise the style of play, which was practiced by the Runcorn teams. They played the open game, whichwas very pleasant to the spectators, and whice in his opinion was far the best; and enabled the players to pile on a bigger score. If they took the clubs that played packed scrimmages, and lay on the ball and held it, they would find that their scores would not equal the Runcorn score. A balance of 67 goals and 49 tries over opponents wasenormous, when they considered the calibre of the clubs that Runcorn had to face. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Riley seconded the motion which was carried unanimously. Mr. J. Timmins moved and Mr. W. Riley seconded a vote of thanks to the retiring captains, .the umpires and committee for their services during the past season. Mr. P. Speakman C.C. had been nominated for the position of president and as there was no opposition he was unanimously elected with loud acclamation. The Chairman observed that Mr. Speakman had taken great interest in the club for many years, and his interest would continue. The list of vice-presidents was ac- cepted, with the addition of the following names Messrs. Tom Jones, A. Linaker' E. Imison, J. Stokes, Dr. Gas- taldi, J. Timmins, and A. Lightburu. The following officers were re-appointed unopposed : H. Hughes, captain of first team ; W. Faulkner, vice- captain; W. H. Cawtey, captain second team ; J. Sherlock, umpire second team ; C. Pownall, Areasurer ; J. E. Langshaw, secretary ; A. Riley, assistant captain ; Messrs. W. Wright and G. T. Wainwright were nomin- ated for the position of umpire, and the voting resulted in a tie of 25 votes. Another vote was taken and Mr. Wright was appointed by 25 votes to 24. The voting for auditors was as follows :—Edward Lunt 31, Edward Key 29, Edward Ridge 23, John Goodwell 23, and the first two were declared elected.—There were 24 nominations for 12 members of the Committee, and the voting re- sulted : W. Carroll 49, W. Hughes 45, John Lunt 44, Walter Jones 43, J. Gatley 43, J. H. Crompton 38, J. Watson 35,W. Riley 29, G. T. Wainwright 28, J. E. Booth 28, James Clarke 27, T. Moore 25 (these were elected), S. Abram 20. H. G. Andrews 21, F. W. Han- cock 11, J. Lewis 12, J. Turnbull 13, Gr. Lea 8, T. H. Davies 16, J. W. Brazendale 14, George Ward 12, P. Riley 21, W. H. Broady 16, and S. Booth 6.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at the Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday afternoon. There were present Major Wareing (ohair- m m), the Rev. C. W. Wooll, the Rev. S. A. K. Sylvester, Messrs. C. B. Johnson, J. Leatherbarrow, J. Mercer, J. Marsh, J. Whalley, G. Davies, J. Peover, J. Goldsworth, G. E. Chadwick, J. Birchall, W. Middlehurst, H. Hulme, J. Ransom, W. Lowe, W. Burrows. J. Burchall, J. Ken- wright, W. Tyrer, J. Griffiths, R. A. Graves, Mr. S. H. Hartley (clerk), and Mr. J. J. Henley (her Majesty's inspector). INMATES.—The Master (Mr. Hale) reported that there were 488 inmates in the workhouse this week, 492 in the preceding week, and 508 in the corresponding week last year. There had been 69 vagrants relieved during the week, against 84 in the corresponding week last year. The Chairman: That is very satisfactory. THE ORGANIST'S SALARY.—A letter was read from Miss Ada Barton, the organist of the Worksouse chapel,apply- ing for an increase of salary.—The Clerk : Miss Barton is organist for both the Church of England and the Catholics in the house.—The application was referred to the Finance Committee.

- GIFTS.—The Chip lain (the Rev. B. A. W. Norris) acknowledged with thanks useful parcels of books for the use of inmates from the Rev. C. F. Aked, St. Helens; Mrs. E. Jones, Knotty Ash; Mrs. Crook, Huyton ; Mrs. Gaskell, Huyton ; Mr. Brown, Prescot; and Mr. R. G. Brook, St. Helens. THE BOYS HomE.—The Clerk said he had a certificate from the architect stating that thesum of £349 17s. 10d. was due to Mr. Davies, the contractor for the Boys Home and the extension of the workhouse. Mr. Leather. barrow moved, and Mr. Lowe seconded, and it was carried, thpl a cheque for £3OO be drawn. THE GUARDIANS AND THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD.— Mr. J. J. Henley (Government Poor Law Inspector), attended in reference to some correspondence between the Guardians and the Local Government Board, with regard to the investment of two sums of money belong- ing to the parishes of Eccleston and Windle, and of which the Guardians were the trustees. Mr. Henley stated that some time ago, by the direction of the Guar- dians, the Clerk asked the Local Government Board to issue an order enabling the Guardians to pay over the money to the current credit of the parishes. The Local Government Board replied that they had no power to do that, as the Act of Parliament compelled them to call upon the Guardians to re-invest the money for the per- manent interest of the parishes. But in spite of that, the Guardians took upon themselves to pay the money over to the parishes.--The Clerk (Mr. Hartley) stated that the exact amount which had accumulated was £3OO Bs. 6d., and in May, last year, the sum of £194 10s. 10d. was credited to Eccleston township, and the sum of £135 17s. Bd. was credited to Windle.—Mr. Hen- ley said that ha e been done against the intimation of the Local Government Board that the money was to be re-invested. He suggested that the matter should be left to the Local Government Board, and the subject dropped. PAUPERISK.—Mr. Henley afterwards stated that he had prepared a return of the pauperism of Lancashire, show- ing the items for each Union. In regttrd to the county during the last ten years he found that although there had been a vast increase in the population, the gross number of paupers in receipt of indoor and out- door relief was smaller now than was the case, ten years ago. The proportion - of paupers to the popula- tion, according to the census returns, was ten years ago one in every 32 of the population, but in 1890 there was only one pauper to every 51 other persons. He was sorry to find that the Prescot Union aid not com- pare very favourably with other unions. They might have a population which required much more relief than was the case elsewhere, but it was the fact that while the average tor Lancashire was one pauper in every 51 per- sons the population in the Prescot Union was one in every 31 persons. There was no Unions in Lanca- shire which stood so badly off as that. They found their proportion of outdoor to indoor relief was very large, and that might be the cause of the blot. On the Ist January last they had 771 indoor poor and 3,018 outdoor poor, while he found in some Unions that the indoor, and outdoor poor were pretty nearly balaneed.—Mr. James Burchall said the nature of the employments at St. Helens and'Widnes were such as to necessitate considerable expenditure in outdoor relief —The Clerk pointed out that there was no outlet for female labour,' owing to their being an entire absence of cotton mills, Btc., and Mr. Davies stated that

there was also very little outlet for boys and youths. Mr. Henley stated that the Board would receive a copy of his return in the course of a few days, and, in responding to a vote of thank, he added that the poor-law funds were nothing but a fund wrung out of the poorest ratepayer as well as the richest, and every Board of Guardians should take care that not a single farthing of that money was spent in an improper manner. RUNCORN SHOOTING CLUB. A match between the shooting clubs of the 2nd Cheshire Railway Engineer Volunteers, Crewe, v. F and G Companies 2nd Cheshire R.V. Runcorn, took place on Saturday, at Holmes Chapel, ten men a side, at the usual distances, 200, 500 and 600 yards, seven shots at each. Queen's regulations. The wind was very tricky, and accounted for some of the small scores. Sapper J. Surridge and Sapper Bretherton were at the top with 88 points each, whilst Sergeant Edwards, be- longing to the visiting team, finished with 84, and Colour-Sergeant Mort 83. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of Widnes School Board was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday afternoon. The Rev. Father Clarke (vice-chairman) presided, and there were also present Dr. O'Keeffe, Dr. McDonnell, Major Wareing, Messrs. 11.11. Davies, H. W. Deacon, B. Brown, C. E. Barlow, and G. H. Danby (clerk).

div.head: DISTRICT EDUCATION ,COMSLITTEE„
div.p: DISTRICT EDUCATION ,COMSLITTEE„

This Committee reported that during the month of April (four weeks) the number of cases summoned be- fore the Committee were the following, viz. :—Applica- tions for payment of fees, 178 ; for contravention of Education Act, 230. Fees were recommended to be paid in 181 cases; refused 17; number of prosecutions before the magistrates 52 ; number of convictions 52. The report was adopted.

div.head: TENNIS AT WEST EA.-TEE HOLIDAYS.
div.p: TENNIS AT WEST EA.-TEE HOLIDAYS.

The School Management Committee's minutes read as foll3ws :—Letter from Miss A. Ward, dated April 30th, 1890, asking for use of West Bank playground for Tennis Club, —The School Management Committee beg to report that, after further consideration, they have arranged for the holidays, at the schools this year to be as follows, viz. :—Whitweek and three weeks at midsummer, com- mencing at noon on Friday, June 27th, and ending on the morning of Monday, July 21st. 1890.—Mr. Brown said the Committee preferred to leave the decision as to allowing the use of the playground at West Bank for tennis to the Board, though the Committee were in favour of the application being granted, subject to a charge and with the necessary protection of the pro- perty. He moved that the application be granted.—Dr. McDonnell seconded the proposal, remarking that the game of lawn tennis was a pleasant and healthy one. West Bank was unfortunately so far away from any place of outdoor amusement, that it was awkward for the residents there to spare the time to reach them. The use of the playground would be a great boon, while the premises would not be injured thereby.—The Chairman could not see any objection to the application which was granted unanimously, a charge of 10d. being made each time the ground was used according to the fixed scale.— The suggestion of the Committee as to the holidays was also adopted. •

div.head: SITES AND BUILDINGS COMMITTEE.
div.p: SITES AND BUILDINGS COMMITTEE.

The minutes of this Committee contained a recommen- dation that the tender of Messrs. Lea and Sons, dated May 12th, 1890, be accepted for the painting, cleaning, and repairs, required at the Warrington-rd. and West Bank schools, and that Mr. Sutcliffe's, dated May 12th, 1890, be accepted for those at Simm's Cross schools, as per architect's specifications. The Committee also re- ported that they have had before/them the notice from the Local Board to level, pave, and flag round the Warrington-rd. schools referred to them by the last Board meeting and they beg to report that they have carefully examined the plan and revised the estimate of the surveyor, which amounted to £194. They have arranged for the Local Board to du the work and to ex- tend the cost over three years, paying the first instalment of £BO in November' 1890, the second of £BO in Novem- ber, 1891, and the balance in November, 1892. Any interest charged by the Local Board not to exceed £4 per annum.—The minutes were adopted.
FINANCE.
The Finance Committee-rec-ommended payment of accounts amounting to £1.002 15s. Bd. Since their last report £149 19s. 7d. for school fees, &c., had been paid to the bank.—Adopted.
A STRONG HINT TO THE OVERSEERS.

The Clerk reported that the treasurer to the Board had written saying that the Board's account was over- drawn by £340. Upon this intimation the rinance Com- mittee at once wrote to the overseers and the following reply has been received from Mr. Goff, the assistant overseer :--" I am directed by the overseers to say that the precept of the School Board will receive their atten- tion as soon as a rate can be levied for that purpose." The Clerk added that after the accounts that had been passed that day were paid the treasurer's account would be overdrawn by £l.3oo.—The Chairman It is a serious matter.—Dr. Olieeffe said the reply of the assist- ant overseer was not at all satisfactory. Hethought the positions ought to be reversed—their clerk was more entitled to write a nasty letter to the overseers than was the assistant overseer to write to them. Considering that the notice of the precept was given in January and that the Board had kept it as low as they possibly could he thought the overseer ought to have endeavoured to let them have something before now. It did not seem as though the overseers had used any efforts ; they were treating the Board as though it was begging something from them, and as though they could give it them when they liked. He did not wish to suggest harsh measures, but he remembered that a number of years ago the pain- ful duty was incumbent on the Board of taking legal proceedings against the overseers, and unless the Board was supplied with the funds requisite to carry on the education department they would have to do the same again. He would, however, make no application to that effect,' just then, but he would suggest that they let the matter stand over until the next meeting, and if a more satisfactory reply was not forthcoming to their demand they would be obliged to take measures much against their will, to compel the overseers to give them the necessary funds.—The Chairman: We cannot go on without funds.—The subject then dropped.p This was all the business. ,

div.head: RUNCORN pErrY_SESSIONS.
div.p: RUNCORN pErrY_SESSIONS.
MONDAY.—Before Mr. C. Reynolds, and 311.7. G. L. Wig°,-- DRUNIENNESS.—Louisa Murray, and John Travis, were each flned. ss. and costs, for this offence.

LICENSES—Thomas Heath-barton, of the George Inn, Poole-lane was granted permission to sell at the Old Bridgewater Arms, Waterloo-road, and Samuel Davies was granted permission to sell at the George Inn. CHIMNEY ON FraE.—Peter Connell was fined ed. and costs for permitting the chimney of his dwelling to be on Are.

UmsiuzzLED Doas.—T. H. Wolsteneroft of Castle Inn, Halton, was fined 6d. and costs for permitting his dog to be at large unmuzzled, and S. Jones of Weston was fined 6d. and costs for having two dogs unmuzzled and a similar penalty for keeping the animals without a license.

A QUESTION OF Juiltsracriow.—E. Watts. shoe dealer, of Church-st., was summoned for assaulting Martha Gumbleton, aged 15 years, daughter of a shoemaker. Mr. Humphreys appeared for the complainant, and from his speech it appeared that at present the defendant'n father occupied the shop and Gumbleton the dwelling-house and about half-past six on the evening of the 6th May, the defendant unlocked the door leading from the shop to the sitting-room. The complainant was alone in the place, and the defendant threatened that if she did not go out he would put her out; and she declined to go, and the defendant attempted to carry out his threat. In the struggle she was considerably Mused and bruised, and she was quite exhausted when her father appeared on the scene and prevented further violence. The only question that could be raised was justification. It seemed Gumbleton carried on business on the premises under a lease, dated 1888 and some nine months ago he got into pecuniary difficulties and made an assignment for the , benefit of his creditors and defendant's father was the purchaser of the stock. A dispute arose as to whether Gumbleton should remain on the premises and Mr. Bur- ton solicitor, wrote telling him to "clear out," but Gumbleton did not take any notice of the request—Mr. , Briggs, solicitor, of Manchester, submitted thatthe mag- istrates had no jurisdiction, as Watson senior was the tenant of the premises and the complainant's father had no right there at all.—Mr. Humphreys said he was placed In rather an awkward position as Mr. Ashton was agent for the property, as well as magistrates' clerk.—The Chairman appealed to Mr. Ashton for the law, and Mr. Ashton replied that the magistrates jurisdiction was ousted.—The Bench then dismissed the case.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COMIT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COMIT.
MONDAY.—Before Messrs. G. --(Chairman) and
11. Giskell, jun.

, DELINIEENNESS.—Ann Carney; Farnworth ; Margaret Haverty., no residence ; William Hall, Ann-st., Manches- ter ; John Cawley, Runcorn; Annie Martin, Pleasant-s. ; and James Tierney, Lugsdale-rd.; were each fined ss. and

costs, or in default seven days, for being drunk and dis- orderly. THE MUZZLING ORDER.—Horatio Syred, pawnbroker, Waterloo-rd., Widnes, and Alfred Ward, Waterloo-rd., were each ordered to pay a fine 2s. 6d. and 7s. 6d.costs for a breach of the Rabies Order, by allowing their dogs to be at large unmuzzled. A NUISANCE AT WEST BANK. Six youths, named Austin Bali, White-st. ; John Bold, Bank-st. ; Albert Jackson, Irwell-st. ; Thomas Marshall, Mersey-rd.; George Wilson, Bank-terrace; and Benjamin Youd, Mersey-rd., were each summoned for obstructing the footpath in Hartland-st., Widnes, on the 4th inst.—P.C. Davieson proved the case and said he had frequently had complaints from tradesmen in the district owing to their conduct.—Ball and Youd, who did not appear, were each fined 2s. 6d. and costs, and the other defendants were each ordered to pay is. and costs. • I WELL ACQUAINTED WITH GAOL.—Catherine Hynes, Nelson-st., was charged in custody with committing a breach of the peace in Sankey-st., Widnes, on the 18th inst.—lnspector Keighley said the prisoner had been before the Court 24 times previously, and had only just come out of gaol after serving a month for a similar offence. She was bound over for a period of three months, or in default of sureties for her good behaviour to go to gaol for three months. ThErr or A WATCH.—Andre Danovitch, a sailor, of no fixed abode, was charged on remand with stealing a silver watch and chain, value 355., the property of John Opperham.—Both the prosecutor and the prisoner are Poles, and on the night of the 19th inst. they were drink- ing together at the bar of the Wellington Hotel, when the prisoner began to talk about the prosecutor's watch and chain. While the piosecutor had the watch in his hand, the prisoner snatched it from him and ran away. He was not seen or heard of until Monday last, when he was arrested in Liverpool.—The prisoner, who said he had bought the watch for £l, was fined £2, or in default of payment 14 days.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THCRSDAY.—Before Mr. H. Gaskell jun., and Mr. J. Brock. Datrior AND-DISORDERLY.—For this offence a fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon the following :—Wm. Brotham, Joseph Jones, Thomas A. Burton, and John MacMalin, William Hunt, and Sophia Eastham were each fined 7s. 6d. and costs.—MaryMullarkey,James Sim- mott and Morgan Connolley were charged with committing breaches of the peace. and were each bound over to be of good behaviour for three months. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE —About 40 parents were sum- moned for neglecting to send their children regularly to school and a fine of ss. was imposed in each case. Several children were committed to the Truant School at Liverpool. Uszmzunn DOG.—John Hall, Mersey-st., was fined 2s. 6d. and costs for allowing his dog to be at large un- muzzled. TRESPASS AT Boar.—Cbaries Stanley, Alfred Hardy, James Bent, and George Steel. of Sutton, pleaded guilty to having on the 4th inst. trespassed on the L. and N.W. Railway at Bold. Each defendant was fined ss. and Costs. SLEEPING Our.-1 tramp named James Molyneux pleaded guilty to sleeping in an outhouse belonging to Mr. T. Astles, of Albert-road, and he was sentenced to 14 days hard labour.

WIDNES FOOTBALL CLUB: ANN UAL MEETING. The annual meeting of the members of Widnes Football Club was held in the Assembly room of the Conservative Club. on Tuesday night. There was a good attendance, and Mr. H. Wade-Deacon, J.P., presided. The Secretary (Mr. Chadwick) read the report, which showed that the first team had played 39 matches, won 14, drawn 5, and lost 20. The "A " team had played 25 matches, won 12, drawn 3, and lost 10. The fit team had scored 23 goals' 44 tries, and 75 minors, to their opponents 24 goals, 39 tries, and 68 minors. The " A " team had scored 15 goals, 27 tries, and 66 minors, to their opponents 17 goals, 29 tries, and 53 minors. The report went on to state the season's performances for the first team had been more inconsistent than those of any previous season. At home (except in League matches) excellent form was shown, but away from home the results were very unsatisfactory, as out of 18 matches played, one was won by a kick, one was drawn and the remaining 16 were lost. If their list of fixtures was to be improved, better form than this would have to be shown when visiting the grounds of their opponents. In matches such as Mossley, Wigan, Warrington, and Tyldesley, when good results would have been of value to the Club, the team managed to score 2 tries and 2 minors against their opponents' 4 goals, 8 tries and 13 minors. The League matches had been a failure, the team losing all hope after the unsatisfactory decisions of the Lanca- shire County Referees' Committee re Wigan match, and the West Lancashire Union League Committee re Hard- man, playing for St. Helens. The County Referees' Committee ruled our appeal as being too late, anct allowed Wigan a try. The West Lancashire Committee, after considering their claim, decided that Hardman, be- ing a junior player, was eligible to play for St. Helens. To this decision the committee of the club would not sub- mit, and unanimously decided to withdraw from the West Lancashire Union. After a brief reference to the tour in Yorkshire, and the Eastertide successes at home, the report stated that J. Clarke had scored 14 tries, D. Brennan 8; H. Peters, 5; J. E. Far- rell, E. Gordon, J. Holt, G. Howard, G. F. Plumpton and J. H. Smith 4 each ; T. McGurl, P. E. Parkinson, and W. Kiddie, 2 each; J. Gandy, G. Hewitt, T. Laws, S. Morris, W. Stubbs and J. Whelan, 1 each. Although 80 new members had subscribed to the club the old members had turned up so badly that an increase was almost invisible.—After is brief discussion the report was adopted.—The Treasurer (Mr. Ashall) then submitted his report. The receipts amounted to £495 4s. Bd. including £424 2s. 4d. gate-money and £6l 9s. members' subscrip- tions. The expenditure was £621 6s. Bd., the principal items being railway and hotel expenses, both teams, £96 3s. 2d.; field and ground expenses, £66 2s. 10d. ; telegraph, postage, printing,and £Bl is. 11d., half-gates returned to Maindu, Barrow Morecambe, Penarth, and Wortley, £39 45. Bd. • fleldnien, chequers, policemen, referees, &c., £43 19s. dd.; teas and refresh- ments, both teams, £36 12s. ld.•, accounts still to pay, £44 10s. 6d., leaving a deficit of £26 2s. 9d. This report was also adopted. On the proposition of Mr. P. Corns, seconded by Mr. A. Lock, it was resolved that subject to the consent of the Lancashire Cousity Committee the sum of £lO be paid to Mr. Ashall in recognition of his past services, and that future treasurer be paid the sum of £7 10s. per annum ; and that the secretary's salary be reduced to a similar amount. Mr. H. Wade Deacon was re-elected the president; and the list of vice-presidents was accepted en-bdoe with the addition of the names of Mr. Peter Longton, and Mr. W. Ireland. The following officers were elected I by tia,lloti—Captain first team, J. Smith; sub-captain, D. Brennan ; captain 2nd team, T. Minton ; sub-captain F. Parr ; hon sec., A Chadwick; sec., F. Younge ; trea., J. Ashall. The committee consists of Messrs. J. A. Brown, A. Huytnn, H. Rose, T. Fogg, P. Corns, T. Bold, J. E. Farrell, C. Hemingway, and J. J. Latham. A new set of rules had been drawn up by a committee specially formed for the purpose, and on the proposition of Mr. J. 114 Smith, seconded by Mr. I. Chadwick, they were adopted. Two propositions were made to alter the club colours, but it was decided to continue to distin- guish the players by a white jersey and black hose. On the proposition of Mr. H. G. Upward, seconded by Mr. A. M. Smith, it was resolved that all accounts passed by the Committee be signed by the chairman and bear the stamp of the Widnes Football Club. It was decided on the motion of Mr. T. Hewitt, seconded by Mr. E. Gordon, that the club arrange a match, the proceeds to be divided amongst the junior clubs of the town.— The meeting concluded with customary vote of thanks.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO MR. H. HUGHES.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO MR. H. HUGHES.

While the scrutineers were engaged in another room counting the votes which would decide who should I,rm the Committee, an interesting ceremony took place. The playing members and a few others had subscribed to form a fund for making a present to the captain of the first team, Mr. H. Hughes, in recognition of his long and valuable service. Mr. Picken, of Bridge- street, had taken artistic and life-like portraits of the members of the first fifteen, and these had been placed in a handsome mounting and enclosed in a carved polished oak frame, the whole making a most effective and appropriate picture. In making the presentation, the Chairman said Mr. Hughes had piloted the club for nine or ten years with very great success—(applause)— and especially during the past year, which had been un- precedented in the history of the club. (Applause.)— After stating that the Rugby Union had granted per- mission to make the present, the Chairman made the presentation amid ringing cheers.—ln acknowledging the gift, Mr. Hughes said he should always be proud of the picture for one reason, because it contained the photo of the best individual scorer in England —(applause)—and not only that, but it also contained one of the best com- binations, if not the best, in England. (Applause.)—ln response to a call from the Chairman, Mr. T. Clegg said a few words, in which he eulogised the personal charac- ter, andthe abilities, of Mr. Hughes, especially with refe- rence to football. After this incident a committriewas appointed to draw up rules for the club, and the meeting terminated.
