THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUN CORN, &c. BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

The inquiry into the police administration of Cheshire is still sub judice and discussion i out of place, but one cannot help feeling, after reading the proceedings as far as they have gone, that the inquiry will " cost something." The first day's pro-- ceedings were carried out at an expense of 1:50; and on the second day the chairman,in endeavour- ing to expedite matters, stated that the inquiry was costing ss. a minute. As the Committee were sitting for six hours that day, the expense would be• £9O, or a total of £l4O for two days. When the Committee resume, they intend to take evidence from day to day until it is concluded, and the total cost, forming an estimate from the above experience, will be over .£l,OOO. • _ _

Mr. George Marshall, chemist and druggist, of Devonshire-square, is about to retire frora the business, which he has conducted for the past 30 years: and in future will devote himself to the work of the Gospel Mission which he has founded in Dukes Field. years ago, Mr. Marshall took a prominent part in the town's affairs as Commis- sioner, Guardian, ttc., and actively participated in many an exciting and lively incident. We wish him health and happiness in his retirement. The Local Government Board are alparently not in a hurry to give a decision on Mr. Jones's appli- cation for a fresh election of Guardians at Run- corn, because of the large number of people who were debarred from voting, although fully en- titled to do so. Perhaps the Board will deliver itself of a weighty judgment about the time the next election approaches. In this warm weather, we are afraid Mr. Jones could not stir them up to exertion, even with one of his charac- teristic and caustic communications.

Football must be a most expensive pastime. Popular as the winter game is in Runcorn and Wid- nes, the clubs of those towns do not seem to gather in the merry sixpences in such sufficiency as to make them able to roll in wealth like one or two of the Yorkshire clubs, or to be even able to meet their liabilities with ease. With an income of nearly £7OO, Runcorn have just about met their expendi- ture, and Widnes, with receipts amounting to about £5OO, are over £2O to the bad. What the clubs evidently want is less shouting and more money.

div.head: LATE MR. J. G. McMISNIES.
div.p: THE LATE MR. J. G. McMISNIES.
A TRIBUTE FROM WORKPEOPLE.

A beautiful permanent wreath has lately been placed in Warrington cemetery as a tribute of the esteem and respect in which the late Mr. McMinnies was held by his workpeople at Farrington. The wreath surmounts a massive square base of finely polished marble, and is placed by the side of the monument over the vault in which the remains of the deceased gentleman lie. On one of the sides of the base are engraved the words "As a tribute of esteem and respect by his workpeople at Farring- ton." The wreath, which is protected by a glass globe, has been very tastefully designed, and con- sists of permanent imitations of roses, lilies, forget- me-nots, and other flowers, encircled with mosses. This tribute of workpeople' s esteem and respect is, without doubt, one of the handsomest and most striking monumental devices in the cemetery. Its placing in the cemetery was witnessed by eight of the managers and principal employes from the mills at Farrington. It may, perhaps, be here mentioned that there is just now a very attractive display of sylvan and floral beauty at the cemetery. Among the flowers which please the eye on all sides are the yellow bloom of the laburnum and broom, the blossoms of the red and white hawthorn, and the varied tints of the rhododendrons. The trees and shrubs, too, are in full foliage, and at many points cast a pleasing shade over the well-kept paths.

div.head: ST. PAUL'S CHURCH, WARRINGTON.
div.p: ST. PAUL'S CHURCH, WARRINGTON.

On Thursday evening a special re-opening service was held in St. Paul's Church, Warrington, which has recently been re-decorated and improved. The organ, which is a very fine one, has been removed from the west gallery to the south-east end of the church, immediately behind the choir stalls, where it will be better heard than was the case when in its old position besides being of more aid to the choir. The church has been generally renovated, re- painted, and re-decorated, and looks considerably im- proved. The cost of the alterations and improvements amounts to £3OO, and the money appears to have been well spent. The work of removing the organ was en- trusted to the capable hands of Messrs. Jardine, Man- chester; the decoration work was carried out by Messrs. Hesketh and Son, and the rest of the improvements were under the charge of Messrs. W. Gibson and Son. A large congregation assembled at the opening service. The prayers were read by the Vicar, the Rev. S. Wilkin- son, and the Rev. G. D. Wray, Vicar of Halton ; the first lesson by the Rev. H. J. Smith, and the second by the Rev. F. W. Willis, Rector of Warrington, and amongst those present were the Rev. Canon Eyre, Vicar of St. Helens, Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Vicar of Holy Trinity, Warrington; Rev. J. Rigby, St. Peter's, War- rington; and the Rev. I. Phillips. The sermon was preached by the Rev. Canon Eyre, who referred to the I alterations that had been made, and dwelt upon the advantages to be gained by the introduction of music into the services of the church. A special anthem was I effectively rendered by the choir, the solo being well sung by Miss Jones. The services will be continued on Sunday.

div.head: SHOPBREAIUNG AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: SHOPBREAIUNG AT WARRINGTON.

On Tuesday night a thief or thieves broke into the premises of Messrs.W. P. & W. Skelton, ironmongers, of liorsemarket-st., and stole a quantity of cutlery, several revolvers, and other goods. They seem to have gained access to the building by climbing the large 4:ate, which form an entrance fr3m Lyme-st. Thence au entrance was forced through ~vindows at the rear of the shop. The premises were securely locked up at a quarter past nine on Tuesday evening, and on being opened at eight o'clock. next morning the counting house was found in a state of great disorder. The desk and floor were strewn with papers and documents ; the drawers, both in the office and shop, had been ran-- sacked ; and the tills emptied of their contents. Amongst the goods missing from the shop. are four ' revolvers, valued at 355. each, and a number or cases of cartridges, fitting the revolvers. A pair of half-worn socks were found on the floor of the counting-house, but, on the other hand, a dozen or more pairs of stockings and socks had been stolen. On a desk was found a loaded revolver, and it is supposed that it was loaded with the intention of its being used should the thieves be disturbed. Two men have been apprehended at Birkenhead with some of the stolen property in their possession, and they will ultimately be brought up at the Warrington Borough Court, charged with having stolen the articles.

div.head: CAPTURE OF THIEVES AT BIRKEEHEAD.
div.p: CAPTURE OF THIEVES AT BIRKEEHEAD.

At the Birkenhead Police Court, yesterday morn- ing, before Mr. Preston, the stipendiary magistrate, George Bennett and Frederick Foster, two men of rough-looking appearance, were charged with breaking and entering the lock-up shop of Mr. Albert Cole, grocer, 452, New Chester-rd., Tranmere. —Superintendent Clarke stated that that morning,. abont one o'clock, whilst P.C. Moore was on his beat and passing Mr. Cole's shop, he heard a noise, and on going into the back yard he found in the water-closet a pair of boots. Suspecting someone was in the shop, the officer whistled for assistance, and Inspector Waugh and P.C. Ravenhill came up. Constable Moore then went over the wall and found the back kitchen window had been broken, after which he and the other officers entered the shop and found the prisoners, one of them with a loaded six-. chamber revolver in his hand, whilst the other, on being searched, was also found to be:- carrying a similar weapon. On the previous even- ing, Superintendent Clarke added, he had received a communication from the Warrington police report- ing a case of shop-breaking there on Tuesday night or Wednesday morning, resulting in the disappear- - ance of a large amount of property, including a, , number of razors, four six-chambered revolvers, a quantity of ball cartridges, some pairs of boots, and other goods, and a considerable portion of this pro- perty, including the two revolvers, had been found upon the prisoners. Police constable 75 then stated that when he met the prisoner Bennett in the shop • he said to him (the officer) that it was a clean cap- ture. He then put his hand into his breast pocket and pulled out a revolver, and said he had better , quieten one or two of them ; upon which Inspector Waugh caught hold of the rev olve,r„and then put the handcuffs on Bennett. The other prisoner was, caught in another part of the shop, and he gave loaded revolver up. Both men were taken to the bridewell, and a number of the other articles re- ported to be missing from Warrington were found • upon them. Evidence having been given by Inspector Waugh, his Worship, at the request of • Superintendent Clarke, remanded the prisoners for a week for inquiries.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
ALLEGED Rona y FROM A FLAT.

William Norman was charged at the Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, with having stolen a quantity of rope, value 4s. 6d., from a flat in the Sankey canal, the property of John Burton. It was alleged that Norman was discharging the flat, and he took the rope away and sold it to a hawker in Warrington. The defence was that the rope was given to prisoner by the hand of the flat. The magistrates imposed a fine of 10s. and costs, £2 9s. 6d. in all. A TICKETLESS TRAVELLER. _ _ - _ _

Samuel Wilcock, a young man who hailed from Liver- pool, was brought up at the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday morning, on a charge of having travelled from Liverpool to Warrington, on the Cheshire Lines Railway, without having paid his tare. When tickets were col- lected at the Central Station, Warrington, on Monday afternoon, prisoner was found in a train. He had not a ticket, and said that he had lost it on the platform at Liverpool. He was ordered to pay a fine of 10s. and costs, the alternative being 14 days' imprisonment. THE CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT. An alleged offence under this Act was investigated at the .Warrington Police Court on Thursday morning, when a man named William Roberts, who lived in Rose and Crown-st., was charged with having assaulted a girl named Emily Bassett, aged 13 years and 7 months, who was in his employ as a domestic servant. During the hearing of the case it was stated that the prisoner and his wife, a lodger, and the girl Bassett, all slept in the same room. Prisoner was committed for trial. Mr. J. 1.. Whittle, the Town-Clerk, conducted the prosecution, and Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins defended.

div.head: THEFT BY A LODGER.
div.p: THEFT BY A LODGER.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Teesday morning, a man named John Lowe, a labourer at Dallam forge, pleaded guilt y to having, on the Tuesday before, stolen £4 10s. in gold, and 135. in silver, from the dwelling- house of Sarah Silcock, 127, Dallam-lane, where he lodged. Edward Silcock, the son of the occupier of the house, placed the money under his pillow on going to bed. Prisoner slept in the same room, and disappeared early next morning, taking the money with him. He wits apprehended at Wigan. The magistrates sent him to prison for two months, with hard labour.

div.head: ... – A Row AT TOWN'S END.
div.p: ... - A Row AT TOWN'S END.

At the Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wed- nesday, a woman named Elizabeth Mason, or Lightfoot, 'was summoned for having, on the 17th May, assaulted Alfred Stokes. Cross-summonses charged Stokes with haying, on the same date, assaulted Lightfoot and another woman named Margaret Bibby. Mr. A. Browne appeared for Stokes, and said that on the date in ques- tion Lightfoot hit him on the head with a poker. The affair, it seemed, occurred in the neighbourhood of Town's End, and much recrimination took place among the witnesses. The magistrates fined Lightfoot ss. and costs, and dismissed the case against Stokes. AN OWNER WANTED FOR A WATCH. Yesterday morning, at the Warrington Police Court, Gatherine Taylor and Thomas Miskell, two well-known characters, were brought up on remand on the charge of having stolen a watch, from some person unknown under circumstances that have been reported previously. Prisoners were arrested on trying to dispose of the watch at Salford, but as the owner had not been discovered, the magistrates bound prisoners to appear if called upon. Miskell was then charged with having committed a breach of the peace on the 7th inst., and was ordered to find sureties for his future good behaviour. It tran- spired that he made a disturbance, and assaulted Taylor, who, however, refused to prosecute him. THEFT OF FURNITURE AT NEWTON. On Wednesday, at the Warrington County Petty Ses- sions, George Craven, an elderly man, was charged with having stolen a mahogany desk from the office of the Sankey Paper Mill at Newton. James Powell, a young man, was charged with the offence of receiving the desk", knowing it to have been stolen. It transpired that Craven, who is a letter carrier, is also caretaker at the mill in question, and lives on the premises. The manager of the mill missed the desk, and gave information to the police. Powell, when charged with having received the wood, said that had he for a moment thought about the matter he would never have taken thewood from Craven, Craven gave him the wood in return for some kindness he had shown him. Powell, who was defended by Mr. A. Browne, was dismissed, and Craven was remanded to the next Newton Petty Sessions, bail being alloyed. A TICEETLESS TRAVELLER'S CONVICTIONS. At the Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wednes- day, a man named Alexandra Malcolmson was brought up in custody on a charge of having travelled from Edge Hill to Newton-le-Willows, on the 15th inst.. without having previously paid his fare.—Mr. Preston, who ap- peared to prosecute, explained that the original maxi- mum penalty for the offence with which prisoner was charged was 405., and that penalty could not be increased no matter how many previous convictions there might have been. By an Act passed last year, however, the Bench had the power, on a second or subsequent convic- tions, to inflict a penalty of £2O, or imprisonment for one month. Against the prisoner there were seven pre- Vious convictions, and in each case he had been committed to prison in default of payment of the fines imposed. The magistrates now fined him 40s. and costs, or im- prisonment for a month in default. A SOLDIER'S SPREE, . .

On Wednesday morning, at the Warrington County Petty Sessions, Wm. J. Noon, a private in the Cheshire Regiment, was charged with having been drunk at New- ton railway station, on the 19th inst. He was also charged with having assaulted J. Wilde, night inspector, and S. Tumock, a Post Office official. Mr. Preston ap- peared to prosecute on behalf of the Railway Company. Prisoner travelled from Liverpool to Newton-le-Willows by the mid-night train on Monday. He was asked for his ticket at Newton, but refused to give it up, and as- saulted Wilde and Turnock, who were on the station platform. Noon told the magistrates that he was drunk at the time, and did not remember anything about what had occurred. His time of sgrvice in the Army would expire on the following. day. Mr. Preston did not press the case, and, under the circumstances, the magistrates intimated that they would bind him over to come up for judgment at the next Newton-le-Willows Petty Sessions.

div.head: POLICEMEN MAKE MISTAKES.
div.p: POLICEMEN MAKE MISTAKES.

At the meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians, on Wednesday, Mr. Ward, the Workhouse master, reported that.in the middle of the night, a man named John Keating had been brought to the Workhouse by a policeman, who said that he was suffering from paralysis. Next morning, however, it was found that Keating had only been helplessly drunk. On another night, soon after, a woman, named Mary Cooper, was broughl to the Workhouse by a policeman, a pathetic story being told of her having been confined on the highway. The next morning it was again found that it had only been a case of drunken helplessness. The Workhouse master wrote to the Chief Constable complaining of these needless disturbances at the midnight hour. and the Chief Constable had replied to the effect that greater care would be taken in the future to ascertain the real ailments of those who fall into the hands of the police. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Tues- day, a woman named Mary Cooper, last from Salford, was charged with being drunk in Winwick-road at half- past ten on the previous night. The Chief Constable said the prisoner was found lying in Winwick-road in a sad and destitute state, and she looked more like a lu- natic than anything else. She was apparently deranged. Whiskey and brandy were given to het to drink by people living in the neighbourhood, and information of the matter was sent to the police. She was conveyed on the ambulance to the Police Station, where she wasseen by Inspector Cox ; and although she had had some drink he did not consider she was intoxicated. She was subse- quently removed to the Workhouse, as she appeared to be in a dying state and almost delirious. The officers no doubt were anxious to act in a humane manner towards the woman, but he (Mr. Hunt) thought that if he had seen the woman he should have had her in front of a good fire, and not have disturbed the officials of the Workhouse close upon midnight. The nurses were called up, and it was discovered that the prisoner had come from Liver- pool and had had too much drink. She subsequently expressed sorrow for her conduct. He had received a letter from Mr. Ward (Workhouse master), complaining about "people being taken to the Workhouse at mid- night in a drunken state, and that the nurses were say- ing so and so." He had sincA replied to Mr. Ward, and had also sent Inspector Spinks to the Workhouse to explain matters. Only the other night a man was found on Bank Quay bridge between ten and eleven o'clock, and was removed to a coffee tavern. He was considered to be in a dying state, and there was an entire absence of anything like drink. The man was sent to the Workhouse at an earlier hour than the woman in the present case, but no complaint was made to him (Mr. Hunt) till the other day. , In both these cases a 4departure was made from the usual custom of bringing the persons to the Police Station, where, if necessary, they were seen by the police surgeon. In these days they had to be very careful not to leek up a person who was not drunk. If the police had erred at all, they had erred on the side of mercy.—The prisoner was fined Gs. and costs, or seven days' imprisonment.— The Chief Constable : I am very glad Mr. Ward has brought the matter under my notice, and we will take care that the officials are not disturbed. At the imne time, if we feel it to be our duty to send there we shall do so.—Alderman Holmes: I think so too.—The Chief Constable: The institution must be used, not abused.

div.head: WARRINGTON HIGHWAY BOARD.
div.p: WARRINGTON HIGHWAY BOARD.

A meeting of this Board was held at the offices in Sankey-st., Warrington, on Wednesday afternoon. Mr. Royston presiding. The other members present were Messrs. J. C. Routledge, J. Houghton, J. Ker- foot, Davies, P. J. Bate, W. Gough,J. Wright and S. Bent. ELECTIONS.—On the proposition of Mr. Royston, seconded by Mr. Kerfoot, captain T. E. Withington was re-elected chairman of the Board for the ensuing year. Mr. Royston was re-elected vite-chairman, and the Finance Committee was re-appointed, the only alteration in its constitution being that Mr. Walter Gough takes the place of Mr. James Fairclough, who is no longer a member of the Board. MONEY WANTED.—It was stated that the sum of £1,150 was due from the County Council in respect of their con- tribution for the maintenance of main roads. Although several applications had been made by letter for the money, it had not been received, and the remark was made that it would be extremely awkward if it did not cometo hand soon, as otherwise there would not be money with which to pay wages, as the account of the Board at the bank was overdrawn. It was, however, thought that payment would be made within a few days, butit was decided to instruct the Clerk to again write asking for payment. THE ESTIMATES.—The Clerk submitted the estimates of expenditure for the ensuing year. They were as fol- lows :—Ordinary maintenance, £2,603; improvements, £1,432; salaries, £350 ; general expenses, £220; work- ing balance, £400; total amount of estimate, £5,005. To meet this expenditure it was decided to levy a rate of Bd. in the £ in the townships under the jurisdiction of the Board.

div.head: HEAVY DAMAGES FOR SEDUCTION.
div.p: HEAVY DAMAGES FOR SEDUCTION.

In the Queen's Bench on Tuesday, an action was brought by Mrs. Gertrude Knight, widow of a naval officer, against Mr. Louis Enger, the well-known music teacher, and musicial critic, for the seduction of her daughter while the latter was a pupil under him. The defendant was not represented. The Solicitor-General opened the plaintiff a case, &scribing it as the saddest and most serious he had known. Miss Bertha Knight deposed to taking lessons in singing in the year 1887 from the defendant who tried to corrupt her. She resisted his advances until in September, 1888, when she and her mother were at Vienna, and the defendant joined them. He induced her to take wine at supper and it made her sleepy. Defendant that night came to her room and seduced her. There was no defence, and the jury found for the plaintiff, damages:£2,ooo.

div.p: E EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 24, 1890.
CHARGES AGAINST RUNCORN POLICE ADMINISTRATION.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY REVELATIONS.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY REVELATIONS.
The adjourned inquiry into the charges brought by. Mr. Slater Lewis against the County Police ad-
Ministration, with special reference to Runcorn, was resumed at Chester Castle, on Saturday morning, before his Honour Judge Horatio Lloyd, Mr. C. Lister, Mr. J,Beckett, Mr.,Duncan Graham, and Mr.

James' Tomkinson.—Mr. A. Fletcher, solicitor, of Northwich, appeared to represent the Chief Con- stable, and ex-inspector O'Donnell was not profes- sionally lepresented. Mr. Ashton, magistrates' clerk for Runcorn appeared with reference to a
statemtnt made by; Inspector O'Donnell a week ago, and staged there was an imputation that the maps-

trates could be controlled I:iy their clerk, which was not right, as he nsver presumed to advise them except upon points of law. The Chairman.—l think we know enough of Mr. Ashton to be allowed tosay that we•clonathink he would do more than that.
- Mr. Lewis said he was, sorry to have to call the atten- tion of the inquiry to a case of what he considered almost
intimidation.
Jonathan nvey, labourer, Runcorn, an ex-P.C., was then called, and said he had been surnmonedasa witness
to that inqniry. Sergeant Gosling said if he were him hs would have nothing to do, with it. He. also said that
when O'Donnell had fTerved his own ends he would not
care for anybody; and that when he (Flivey) got into the mire or mud, O'Donnell would not help him oat. The . .
sergeant &Ist; told him he was not corAiellecT t& attend the inquiry. The Chief Constable : I deny it is intimidation at all. The Chairman: Be do I, but it is talking:to a witness, ..

which I think we should have a word to sy about. The Chairman (to Gosling) : Did yoir see him and speak to him, and advise him to have nothitr to do with it, and say that as long as O'Ddnnell got his, own ends served he did not care for anybody else ? .
Gosling.—l saw him on-the eFiiday night, and he asked me if he was conspelled. to attend:, anti,l. said, my

opinion was that he writ;, but he could pleaseliimselt. also said that he was no to take my opinion as final. The Chairman.—Did roti say anything about o,Dbn- ;nell that he did not carer for anybody so long as he got his own ends served?

Gosling.—l did, sir; but I advised him to please him. !self and not take my opinion. 1 The Chairman suggested that it was a waste of time to lgo. into these side issues, but said witnesses had' better iabstain from talking to one another hi this. manner ,until the inquiry was over. I\fr. Lewis said he had another letter from a • Saperin- sendeut of Police, in which:be said he dare notrinove in this ease.
The Chairman protested e.qainst this remark; and" said that Mr. Lewis's own knowlecte of the world must show hits, the value of letters of that kind.
Mr. Slater Lewis.—lt does, sir y indeed. Mr. Liswis was proceeding to say that through 'fear these officers dare not move, when

The Chairman interposed, and said they must be governed by some rules of evidence, and must'not be ' governed by tittle tattles of every description. Mr.. Slater Lewis said he was in a very peculiar posi- tioni.as he had to fight for hie evidence as if fighting for his life. He had got the whole police force against him, and when he wanted men of the force to give evidence, he wanted them to come therewith nothing to fear front the Chief Constable or anybody. else, to give their evi- dence-as straightforward men. The is quite right, but in this -parti- cular instance we will abstain from saying what we think,.but I say it had better not occur again, whatever it is. The Chairman intimated. that the members,of the Inquh7 had decided to limit the range of the enquiry over the years 1887, 1888, 1889 , which would • leave a period of eighteen months before and after OPHonnell wenttaliuncorn. This would be done without drawing any hard and fast lines as to going into more., remote dates'oil matters of character and suchlike. Ex4bspector O'Donnell was then re-called.

Mr. Fletcher.—Will you be good, enough to say to whom you. refer by the words magistrates' clerks and solicitors drinking at this hotel 7' I do not third( I used magistrates' clerks at all. I meant magistratesr clerks' assistants, Ike.—To whom do you refer by magistrates' clerks' 'assistants, &c.? FUNERAL OF THE LITE MR. SHERIDAN.

The funeral of the late Mr. Minsley Sheridan, pro- prietor of the Theatre Royal, Scotland-road, took place at the Warrington Cemetery, on Sunday afternoon, the number of spectators being estimated at from 1.200 to 1,300. The funeral procession left 45, Scotland-road, the late residence of the de- ceased, at half-past one, and the Cemetery was reached in about half-an-hour. There were about a dozen private carriages in the procession the route taken' to the Cemetery being through procession, Buttermarket-St., and Church-st. The funeral service was read by the Rector of Warring- ton (the Rev. F. W. Willis). Among those present were Alderman Davies, Harrison, and Wright; Mrs. Sheridan (widow of the deceased) ; Mr. and Mrs. At4inson and family, Leeds: Mr. and Mrs. Sweet- man, Liverpool; Mr. and Mrs. Cavanagh, Man- chester; Mr. and Mrs. Grounds, Warrington.; Mr. and Mrs. Newall, Warrington; Mn and Mrs. Percy Randall, Warrington; Mr. and Mrs. Manning, Warrington; Mr. and Mrs. Bell, Warring- ton; Mr. and Mrs. Porter, Warrington ; Mr. and Mrs. Ohmy, Warrington ; Mr. and Mrs. Smethurst, Warrington; Mr. and Mrs. Thorne and Mr. and Mrs. Jefferson, Theatre Royal, West Hartlepool; Mr. Stanhope and Mr. Voulee, of Theatre Royal, Birken- head; Mr. J. div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse, on Wednesday morning. Alder- man Harrison presided, and there were also present Rev. G. F. Roberts; Messrs. Ratcliffe, Wackhurst, T. Jones, Davies, Jolley, W. Houghton, Smith, Clarke, Kilshaw, Humphries, Warburton, Kilshall, Dobson, J. HoUghton, Dignum, Hood-Wright, Hibbert ; J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), C. H. Ward (workhouse master), and 11. M. Mines (super- intendent of Padgate Schools).

THE HOUSE COMMITTEE. This Committee reconimended the appointment of John Jefferson a pensioner and an inmate of the Workhouse, as male attendant upon lunatics when brought into the workhouse,at a salary of £5 per annum witn uniform and rations; also that Miss G. Wilson, children's attendant, be appointed female lunatic attendant at a salary of £lO a year.—On the motion of Mr. RATCLIFFE, seconded by Mr. Donsort, the minutes were confirmed. SCHOOL FEES.
The School Fees Committee reported that fees had been allowed in 52 cases, 45 of which were old and seven new cases.

- . ELECTIONS. The CLERK reported that he had received orders from the Local Governfnent Board for the election of a guardian for the township of Haydock in place of Mr. Wright, resigned; and for the township of Warrington in place of Mr. Greening, deceased. THE RATING. OF MACHINERY. Two or three communications were read by the Clerk asking the Board to petition against the Rating of Machinery Bill at present in the House of Commons. It was pointed out that the passing of the Bill exempting machinery from taxation would have the effect of very materially lessening the rateable area of the country.— Mr. W. HOUGHTON moved, and Mr. HOOD-WRIGHT secon- ded, that the Board petition against the Bill.—Mr.. RATCLIFFE, who had, upon Alderman Harrison leaving the room, taken the chair, approved of the proposal as he thought the Bill one of the most unjust ever brought I before the House of Commons.—Mr. DIGNT/M asked what effect the passing of the Bill would have upon that Union.—Mr. RATCLIFFE said it would have a great effect in the Earlestown district by reducing the assessments of such places as the Vulcan Foundry and the Viaduct Works.—The CLERK said it was some 20 odd years ago since they went into the question of the rating of machinery in Warrington and at that time the result was that many thousands of pounds were added to the rate- able value of the town. That result was secured without any contests or appeals, but they had had one appeal during the 18 years he had been their clerk, and that was by the London and North-Western Railway Company against the Assessment of their works at Earlestown. The Railway Company were defeated at the Quarter Sessions and had to pay costs. If the Bill referred to were passed it would effect the assessment of the gas and water works and of all the manufactories so far as they used machinery. The rates that were thus lost must i necessarily fall n proportion upon other ratepayers.—lt was decided to petition against the Bill, and the Clerk was also authorised to take what action he thought advisable in opposition to the Bill. This was all the business.

THE LATE MR. T. H. POTTER.

Sir,—ln your notice of Mr. Sheridan's death in last week's "Examiner," you say, speaking of the latter gentleman's appearance at the Princes Theatre, Man- chester, in the pantomime of "harlequin Blackbird," that "the late T. Potter, an actor of repute and a Warrington man, appeared at the Princes at the same time." Allow me to say that this is not correct. My brother never played in pantomime, although he had many lucrative offers to do so. True it is that he ap- peared several times at the Princes with his old and • esteemed friend" Sherry," but not in pantomime. This line of business was not his forte.—Yours truly, .1. POTTER.

div.head: BREWER'S ENDOWMENT BILL
div.p: THE BREWER'S ENDOWMENT BILL

Sir,—The Bill for bribing brewers and beersellers has been before Parliament for some time now, but I have not seen that any action is being taken by the local temperance party to stop the passing of this iniquitous measure. Where are our leading teetotallers that they are keeping so intensely quiet on this subject? Surely if ever a Bill needed opposition this baneful Bill does, and I hope, while there is yet time, some steps will be taken to strengthen the hands of the temperance party in the Rouse of Commons. Publicans are no worse off than tradesmen who are liable to be turned out of their premises at the whim of their landlords, but who ever heard of tradesmen being compensated under such cir- cumstances? Ido trust the Temperance Federation will wake up and call a public meeting so that the feelings of the town can be made known.—Yours, &c., NO COMPENSATION. May 23rd, 1890.

"WARRINGTON AND THE DRINK QUESTION. Sir,—Referring to the case heard, on Monday last, against a licensed victualler, and the remarks made by the magistrates' clerk as to the necessity for a Public Prosecutor, I am surprised that the temperance party in Warrington da not move in this matter. The small num- ber of convictions recorded against publicans is out of all proportion to the number of " drunks " brought up weekly before the Bench. It is the usual thing to read in the papers of cases against licensed victuallers being dismissed, and there is no wonder the police feel dis- heartened in bringing such cases into court. Anyone in the streets, after nine o'clock on Saturday night, cannot help being struck with the amount of drunkenness in the town, and it follows that if people are locked up for being drunk, there is a publican some- where who has supplied the drink, and consequently there should be a conviction in such cases.

I would supplement the remarks of the Masistrates' Clerk as to a Public Prosecutorby saying, that the town, I think, is large enough now to entitle it to the use of a Stipendiary. lam sure the Chief Constable and his offi- •cers do their best to carry out their duties, but the case under notice shows that legal assistance in the person of a Public Prosecutor is required, as the summons was issued wrongly, although I always thought that the Bench possessed power to amend errors of this descrip- tion. Ido not say that the result would have been diffe- rent, but it is not so satisfactory to the public. I have nothing to say against "the trade ;" in fact. I am not a teetotaller, but I cannot help thinking that some steps should be taken to check the drunkenness -existing at present,
ROMAN CATHOLICISM.

div.head: LOOKER ON.
div.p: LOOKER ON.

Sir.—How very edifying is the letter by your correg- pondent " Rangatira." His poetic effusions and puerile 'comparisons are so flagrantly ridiculous, that they are deserving only of the most utter contempt. I would Itivise him to "Secure the substance ere the shadow fade," for unless he is more economical with his kisses, the photo in question will lose its lustre like the toe of a certain statue which I saw in a Romish Church in Barce- lona, which was being constantly kissed in the most affectionate manner.

With respect to the answers of Mr. Williamson, they are so evasive and turn off into such side issues that it is impossible to make either bead or tail of them. He says that the Pope,in the pastoral I quoted in my last letter, is referring to Bibles wrongly translated, which is equiva- lent to saying that the Bibles issued by the British and Foreign Bible Society are wrongly translated. He is at issue here with on of our Archbishops who presided the other day over a great Bible Society meeting, and spoke in terms of the highest praise of the work done by the Society. I refer to the Archbishop of York, who by com- mon consent made the speech of the season at the May Meetings in his noble defence of the British and Foreign Bible Society. Then we have Archdeacon Straton and Capon Scott, who have nobly spoken in its defence re- cently. With regard to his answer as to the infallibility of the Pope, it will take a clever man to dctermine when the Pope is supposed to be infallible. What lam surprised at is that it took so many hundreds of years after Christianity was established to discover tliat the Pope was infallible.

Christ, in the 23rd chapter of St. Matthew, says "One is your Master, even Christ, and all ye are brethren." Paul evidently did not accept the idea of Peter's infalli- bility when he resisted him to his face (1) Gal. 2. ii. St. Augustine, that great and good Catholic (not Roman though) asserts that the Church upon which Christ said he would build His Church is Christ Himself. Pone Gregory Ist says that Christ is Himself the stone from which Peter takes his name. Peter himself says that "Christ is the chief corner stone on which believers are built up a spiritual house." Ist Peter 2. 4-6. So or my- self I prefer to take Christ as my only infallible Pope, seeing that the votaries of the Romish Church are unde- cided as to when and where their Popes are infallible. I am a Catholic, but not Roman. The disciples were first called Christians at Antioch" Acts 11c., 26v. Had I been living in Antioch, I should have been an Antio- chian Catholic, if at Rome a Roman Catholic, (not under Lee's jurisdiction,however)but as I am in Horsforth I am a Horsforth Catholic. Amongst the Apostles. Paul is my ideal man and I consider him head and shoulders higher than Peter in every respect. He himself says," I was not a whit behind the very ehiefest Apostles II Cor. 11c., sv. Moreover, he was the Apostle to the Gentiles, and dwelt at Rome two years in his own hired house, where- as Peter was the Apostle of the Circumcision. It was Paul who wrote the epistle to the Romans where he never mentions Peter amongst those to whom he send saluta- tions. Again Paul,was not the man to go to Reme had Peter been there, for he says I have strived to preach the, Gospel, tint where Christ was named, lest I should build upon another man's foundation. Rom. 1520. Peter calls himself an " Apostle to the strangers scattered through- out Pontus, Galatia, Cappadecia' Asia, Bithynia " but never mentions Rome. Ist Peter lc., lv. "Redtail" appears to dread Scripture. Let him study the follonving from the prophet Isaiah, and with this I close—" To the law and to the testimony : if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them" Is. 8 c. 20 v.—Yours very truly, G. W. HARGREAVES. P.S.—There is just one matter I have omitted. " Red- tail " says their church has stood for centuries pursu- ing the even tenour of her way. So has Mahomme- •danism, Buddism, and many other "isms." but as Thomas Carlyle says, after designating the Pope "the • supreme quack," "the greatest of all gospels is that a Zie cannot endure for ever."

div.head: "MORE FACTS."
div.p: "MORE FACTS."

Sir,—l cannot permit Mr. Williarnson's letter of Sat- urday last to pass without drawing attention to the fan that he has admitted thetruth of the statements I made in my first letter to you. Surely after your _correspon- dent's last epistle, your latest recruit, " Rangatira," will ' be more than.ever inclined to urge Mr. Williamson to withdraw from this controversy. He certainly was no ,belp to Mr. Williamson, notwithstanding his irony and .his comparisons. , I dare say if " Rangatira "had fallen in love, sod had received a photograph of his inamorata, he woti:d have been able to see in %some likeness to the (Meet of his affections; but I defy anybody to malce y semblance of what he cal "Our Blessed Lady" of the hideous gigantic and other erections that I Lave seen stuck up to represent that personage, and especially as no two of them are alike.

As to "Runcorn Redtail" it is as clear as day light, that he has little or no sympathy with the cause he is professing to defend, and his only object seems to be to twit Mr. Foulkes. In your issue of the 3rd ult, Mr. Williamson, while not denying my assertion that Catholic.% worship the Virgin Mary, did • deny that Catholics worship saints, crucifixes and images"- That, said he, " would be idolatry." In your last issue, Mr. Williamson admits that "Catholics glorify .Him in His mother, in His saints, and in His angels, and in the pictures and images of Him, which they keep with respect and veneration." Now, in the fifth edition of Storrnonth's English Dictionary, published by Blackwood, the verb " worship "is thus defined "to pay divine honours to, to adore, to honour highly, to idolise." On this definitiog therefore I contend Mr Williamson has fully demonstrated the truth of the assertion be was so eager to refute, and that the glorify- ing above mentioned is idolatry. It is against this practise and teaching that I protest, for it is altogether contrary to the teaching of the scriptures which say "thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any like- ness, or anything that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth; thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them." Your correspondent declares that "Catholic well know that the Blessed Virgin or the Saints can give us nothing of themselves." Then, if they are so useless, it is simply ridiculous to ask the aid of helpless beings, even to the extent of" merely asking the saints to pray that God may grant them all necessary grace through Christ." I know that if I wanted assistance of any kind I should not appeal to people who "can give us nothing of themselves. I should not think of wasting my time on such individuals, but should go straight to the foun- tain-head. It so happens that this is what all Christians are invited to do. Christ himself affectionately pleads "Come unto Me." There is no need here for saints, symbols, pictures, calvaries, crucifixes, or any other invention to distract our attention from :the Saviour of Mankind. Indeed Christ might have had all these latter things in His mind when He said" No mai cometh unto the Father, except by. Me." . _ _

. . As to " veneration before a picture or imageof Christ,' I have men now a very vivid recollection of a horrible repulsive representation of Christ after the crucifixion (the only representation of Christ I can remember), the like of which I have never seen equalled for ghastliness even in that notorious institution of sensations—the morgue itself. How anybody could feel drawn to venerate Christ after contemplating such a hideous por- trayal passes any comprehension. Though byno means very squeamish on such matters, I turned from the scene with disgust. It is not by such sights as these that people will be won, but by the representation of Christ as He is the son of the True and Living God, ever ready and ever willing to hear and to help all that come unto Him without the intervention of priests, virgins, saints, symbols, or anything elm. Your correspondent accused me of being a victim to "prejudice, passion and error," but I think he has shown by his admissions, that all these undesirable qualities exist in his own breast.—Yours &c.,
A DISSENTER.
ROMAN CATHOLICS AND IMAGES.

Sir,—Not wishing to make my first letter too long, I have deferred to the present an answer to Mr. William- son's second objection. "Catholics do not worship crucifixes, and images. That would be idolatry." lam glad he thinks this latter; but, why does his church so hide the second commandment from the people? Now, as to the term "worship." It will not do to quibble over the word. In the Walker's dictionary it means "To pay divine honours to, to perform acts of adoration or religious service." It is not Protestants who charge Romanists with "paying divine honours" to images: and so " worshipping " them. It is their own church that teaches them to do it ; and nowhere teaches that there is danger or sin in the use of images for religous honour. As for the proof, St. Thomas Aquinas is a Roman Catholic Saint and doctor; hence, he is an authority that cannot be challenged. In his " Summa," the greatest of all Roman Theological works, we read :

"The same reverence should be displayed towards an image of Christ and towards Christ himself; and seeing that Christ is adored with the adoration of Latria (this means, supreme religious worship) it follows that His image is to be adored with the adoration of Latria," again, "The cross is adored with the same adoration as Christ, that is, with the adoration of Latria, and for that reason we address and supplicate the cross just as vie do the crucified Himself," and, "Images of saints may be and ought to be adored with a certain inferior adoration, or ddia. like the saints themselves." Also in Pontificale Roman we read" The Legate's cross shall be on the right because Latria is due to it." To this may be added that in the Breviary and Missal for the Festival of St. Thomas Aquinas there is this prayer—" Grant to us we beseech Thee, to embrace with our understandings what he taught." Romanists pray that they may follow what he taught. 'He taught that supreme religious worship is to be given to images. Therefore Romanists if true to the princiV of theii ch_uro are boup;:i to worship images; and vdry pfOrrittly Mr. William Son Says thiS i 4 " , tory." Romanists oft say that no MOM is intended or their ' images than Protestants intend by the use of painted windows and sculpture in their churches and chapels. This is not true. In Rome there is the Bambino, an image of the Saviour, which is regarded as a wonder-worker. Of old the heathen used to use the very same arguments for their use of images, as Romanists use now. Theysaid they regarded them simply as bringing home to the mind certain attributes of Deity; and on this ground gave them worship. Protestants do not kneel before, or kiss, statues and representations. But what did the Early Christian Writers think of the use of images at all ? Lactantius (300 A.D.) writes 6' Wherever there is an image there is no religion." Minucius Felix (220 A.D.) says, "Crosses, moreover, we neither worship nor wish for." St. Epiphanius 370 A.D., tore up a curtain with an image of Christ on it, because he said it was "contrary to the authority of Scripture, and contrary to our reli- gion." St. Augustine, 4.30 A.D., represents a heathen in saying, "I do not worship that (image), but, I bow be- fore (I adore) what I see, and serve Him whom I do not see." Compare this with what the Council of Trent says, "Through the images we adore Christ and pay veneration to the saints whose likeness tho images bear" and adds St. Augustine, " By giving the explanation of their images, they think themselves clever, as not wor- shippers of Pops Gregory the Great saw the ten- dency of worshipping images which was idolatry develop- ing in his day, 595 A.D., and writing to the Bishop of Marseilles says—" Ix every possible way avoid worship- ping images.'" The Church of Rome in the past was a pure church, but error gained entrance and soon developed ; so that now heathenish practices are sanctioned and followed which in the past were sternly forbidden. " The fine gold has become dim." Cassander, a Roman writer,says "How much the Fathers in the primitive Church did abhor all manner of worshipping images, even Origen, declares against Celsus." In 787 A.D., the second Coun- cil of Nice decreed. "We venerate, worship, and adore the sacred images." "We may, therefore, worship the images, &c." And in 1270 A.D. St. Bonaventure declares, " The same reverence is paid to the image of Christ himself." Bellarmine, Azarius, Cajetan, Almain, some of the highest theologians declare the same. I could bring forward many more proofs confirming the charge we make against the Roman Church, that she fully sanctions the worship of images ; and so becomes involved in the guilt of idolatry. If Catholics do not worship images which their church enjoins them to do, it simply follows that they are not true to the principles of their church. No sin is more a.bhorent to the Almighty than idolatry. At Sinai ho slew thousands of his people for worshipping Him " through " the golden calf ; not for worshipping the calf simply : and centering on it their worship; but for using it in wor- ship at all. Well might holy St. John write : " Little children, keep yourselves from idols."-1 remain, &c., TRUTH. P. 8.—1 have just come across the following prayers— "o Cross. sweet wood! Sweet nails! Save this pre- sent multitude." '0 good cross, receive me from men, and restore me to my Master."

div.head: ROMAN CAT UOLICISM.
div.p: ROMAN CAT UOLICISM.
_ Sir,—ln reply to your correspondents "Runcorn Red- tail," "Rangatira" and Mr. Williamson, I will with your kind penni sqion say a few words as briefly as possible.

4,Redtail" asks me to stick to my assertion about tradition not bearing scrutiny in many cases. Well, if he wishes one or two prnofs, Saint Liguori who wrote the book "Glories of Mary" was made a saint through one of his reported miracles of,curing a woman of a cancer in her breast, through merely looking at a portrait of Liguori and swallowing in medicine a bit of some of his clothing (the doctors had performed an operation by cutting off the breast). The woman went to sleep, , wakened up next morning, found herself cured, and the breast replaced. Next comes the tradition about the coat at Treves, pilgrims to which by getting some article of clothing, medal lac., placed on the coat or allow it to come in contact, come away rejoicing. Such idolatry is condemned in very strong language by Father John Ronge to Bishop Arnold of Treves ; he said "Do you not know—as a bishop you must know—that the Founder of the Christian religion left to his disciples and his successors not his coat but his Spirit? His coat, Bishop Arnold of Treves, was given to his executioners." Drs Sybel and Gildemister, Professors in the University at Bonn, say there were twenty other seamless coats,and their researches contradict, in the plainest manner, the pretensions of the coat at Treves to be a garment worn by Christ. Scripture is against Christ wearing such a long robe (5 feet) Mark 12c 38v. Pope Urban VIII. in 1631 declared in favour of another coat. Pope Nicholas IV. says the Lateran at Rome has it. rope Gregory. XVI. decrees the church at Argenteuil to have it, and yet he sanctioned a pilgrimage to Troves. Tradition was , placed on a level with Scripture only at Council of Trent.

Redtaii asks me "Do I think the gates of heaven ars closed against all Rotnanists, Tractarians). Unitarians ?" Personally I have always admitted that there are better R0M3.1118t9 than their church's creed, to name a few, Martin Booz, Martin Luther, Pastor Chinquy, late Dr. Dollinger, of Germany, and others of all classes. Archbishop Laud said a"churchi may err greatly, nay damnably, in the exposition of it (the funchunental points of Christianity); and this is the Church of Rome's case. There is a great peril of damnation for any man to live and die in the Romish persuasion." Archbishop Brain- hall said "The Church of Rome issno apostolical, ortho- dox or Catholic Church." Archbishop Tillotson said "But as for-those who had the opportunity of coming to the knowledge of the truth, if they continue in the errors of the Romish Church, or apostatize from the truth, I think their condition so far from being safe, that there must be extraordinary favourable circumstances in their case, to give a man hopes of their salvation." Saint Paul tells Timothy that the Scriptures are able to make wise unto salvotion ; not a word about tradition. " Red- tail." and such like, do not approve of quotations. As my letters are for the benefit of your numerous readers and with, 1 hope, a view of arriving at Bible truth it is impossible to leave out its teaching. I ask him and others to read Matt 7c 15-29 compare with John 20c 31. Romish version if they like, and they will see the written Scriptures are commended not tradition. An influen- tial priest admitted " The moment a man searches the Bible for any doctrine he becomes a Protestant. "Rangatira " makes assertions about my knowledge of Romanism, but he fails to disprove one of my state- ments ; his sneers are not argument. Will he say that the Romish Church does not decree, "That Scripture is to be read or interpreted according to the unanimous consent of the Fathers ?" Now as this is a fact, it is impossible for 999 out of every 1,000 Romanists to know the meaning of even one chapter. Take for example Matt. 26, they would require to know Greek and Latin to wade through two hundred folios before knowing what the fathers said; to find after at least twenty years' reading that they were opposed to one another: no un- animity whatever. This explanation about images is rubbish in face of Exodus 20e. The worshippers of the brazen serpent, or the sun, might have made same excuse. " Rangatira:s "advice to Mr. Williamson to withdraw from the controversy is sound, seeing the way Mr. Williamson tries to defend a false system. Mr. William- son's parting sentence to me is nothing to disprove any- thing I have written ; he says, "I am radically wrong again, and no attempt could touch it for errors." Does he mean my quotations from Council of Trent, Roman Missal, Glories of Mary, Garden of the Soul, Catholic " Times,"•lrish "Times," or Feast of Portincula areal! errors; if so I challenge proof; I defy him. Perhaps he will wish us to believe the doctrine of Immaculate Con- ception was decreed before 1854 or Infallibility before 1870. According to Mr. Williamson the Pope is liable to error whenever there is no General Council. As it is twenty years since one took place, he has been falling into error all along. This may account for his not get- ting his predecessor out of Purgatory, for his granting in 1886 to Henry Lassen permission to circulate in France a translation of the four gospels, and in the year follow- ing he cancelled it. Cardinal Richelieu once asked his own ci aplain, "How many masses would serve to fetch any Eill out of Purgatory?" Unable to answer the Ifaietious yet critical question, the Cardinal pleasantly solved it himself, as a dignitary of the church, acquainted with all her Mysteries. " Just so many masses," said he, "would servfto liberate a soul from Purgatory, as it would take of snowballs to heat an oven." Cardinal Perren was asked by some of his friends, in his last sick- ness, what he thought of transubstantiation? He replied "it is a monster." And so say I of the creed of Pope Pius IV, full of curses, whereas Christ's sermon is full of blessing I ask Romanists to accept the Bible truths, not those decrees made by men. Come out of her bond- age. Popery is but a sham. Frodsham, May 20th, 1890.
ROBERT FOULKES.
[We shall permit Mr. Williamson to reply, if he cares to do so, and with his letter we must close the controversy for the present.—F.D. Ex.]

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
THE WARRINGTON HIGHWAY BOARD AND THE CLOSING OF FOOTPATHS.

At a meeting of the Warrington Highway Board, held on Wednesday, a discussion took place with regard to the Manchester Ship Canal (Vsrious Powers) Bill, which, it was stated, proposes to repeal a section of the previous Act of 1885, which safeguarded the Board in regard to the closing of footpaths in the district of the Board. By the previous Act it was provided that, if the Canal Com- pany closed any footpath. they must substitute a new one in its place, and it is now proposed to withdiaw the sec- tion that makes such provision. Mr. Davies, a member of the Board; mentioned that a footpath at Rixton waS in the possession of the company, and had a line of rails on it, but it was stated that it was not thought to be the intention of the company to close the footpath, but to divert it. Ultimately tne further consideration of the matter was referred Lo the Finance Committee.

VISIT OF GEOLOGISTS. On Saturday the Liverpool Geological Society visited the famous tVarburton cutting of the Ship Canal. The cutting is now of the full depth, and presents a most striking appearance, the Eenper marls occupying nearly the whole length of the cutting being beautifully rib- boned with alternations of pale green and bright red marl. The wonderful system of small faults which in- tersects the beds is visible now as it has never been before. Towards the Thelwall end of the cutting it was observed that the marls were smashed to an extraordi- nary extent, and the fissures produced had been filled in with a deposit of gypsum disposed in transverse prisms, rnd it was pointed out that by a further disturbance tak- ing place subsequently to the inning, the prisms had been bent. Beyond the smashed marls a great fault crosses the line of the canal, though it is not at present exposed. This fault must have produced a vertical dis- placement of the rocks amounting to at the least 1,000 feet. At the far end of the cutting an immense depth of river sands and gravel was observed, the product of the Mersey when its course was slightly different from its present one. Many interesting specimens were collected. including slabs showing ripple markings, sun cracks, and last, but not least, the remarkable casts of salt crystals (pseudomotphs), which are still to be found in abun- dance. Much surprise was expressed at the progress which had been made with the werk, despite the mis- haps which have given so much trouble to the coutractnr.. Just opposite the Bankside Paper Mills, a trouble-orne slip has happened, overthrowing a steam navvy and doing other damage, not, however, so serious as that done by the Warburton slip, which has not even yet been cleared away.

div.head: LORD SALISBURY AND STANLEY.
div.p: LORD SALISBURY AND STANLEY.

Mr. H. M. Stanley has conditionally undertaken to lecture in North Wales, on behalf of the Congo House Training Institution for African Children at Colwyn Bay. Speaking at a banquet given on Thursday night by the Merchant Taylors' Company, Lord Salisbury alluded to recent speeches of Mr. Stanley. He warned them against drawing the conclusion that Stanley was behind the scenes, and .was really revealing some secret of the Government tothe British public. The Government had not surrendered anything, for the best reason in the world—that no agreement had yet been arrived at.

RETIREMENT OF GENERAL ' BOULANGER. The Boulangist pipers publish a letter from General Boulanger, in which he announces the dissolution of the National Committee. The General announces that his sole wish now is to live in retirement, and meditate on things accomplished, but at the same time he will always remain a soldier of France and the democracy. General Boulanger has addressed to M. Laisant a letter in which he declares that he desires there should no longer be any intermediary between himself and his sup- porters, and that he therefore pronounces the dissolution of the National Committee. The Boulangist journals reproduce the letter without comment.

div.head: STEAM NAVVIES ON THE SHIP CANAL
div.p: STEAM NAVVIES ON THE SHIP CANAL

This week we re-produce a sketch of the "American steam navvy," which is largely used and has done a mighty work on the Ship Canal. "American steam navvy" is somewhat of a misno- mer. It is true that this very effective piece of mechanism is claimed to be an American inven- tion, but psi the other hand, the claim is by no means admitted by all who have followed the evo- lution of the steam navvy, and it is quite certain that the machines used on the Ship Canal are made, not in America, but by Messrs. Ruston and Proctor, engineers, of Lincoln. It will be seen from the‘sketch, that the American navvy has some points of resemblance to an ordinary steam crane, but also some wide points of divergence. As in the crane, there is a boiler and engine, a revolv- ing roller, and a moveable arm or jib, but there the comparison ends. In the jib of the navvy there is a slot or opening in which is placed a long arm that works ns, and down, upon what is technically known as a rack. To this arm is fixed .a huge bucket,in shape much resembling an ordinary coal scuttle. This scuttle is supplied with four broad knives,or teeth, for cutting into the earth. The whole machine weighs about 20 'tons, and is fixed upon a solid frame with wheels. . When in use, the machine requires three men in direct attendance, namely, a fireman, an engine driver, and a wheel- man; while platelayers and other labourers, to the number of nine, are fully employed in the imme- diate vicinity. On either side of the machine, wagons stand on the railway metals, and imme- diately the bucket is filled it is swung round over a wagon by the jib, the wheelman pulls a string, the, bottom of the bucket swings open, and out falls the earth into the wagon. Each time the bucket scoops up the face of the cutting it carries away nearly two tons of earth, and it is calculated that in the course of an ordinary working day the navvy is capable of removing about 1,200 tons of soil.

div.head: NEW WELSH STEAMERS. THE FIRST TRIP;
div.p: NEW WELSH STEAMERS. THE FIRST TRIP;

The magnificentClyde-buift steamer St. Tudno, which has been placed onsthe Welsh Coast service, made her first trip on Thursday from Liveipool to Llandudno, Beaumaris, and Bangor and back. In the matter of speed and comfort. the St. Tudno gave every satisfaction to the largo and distinguished company on board. Some nautical authorities bad stated that her size would militate against her, that she would be unable to take the Rock Channel when other steamers could do 83, that she could not land passengers at some of the piers, and that she could not turn in the straits. All these evil prognostications were falsified. The St. Tudno left the Landing-stage at 10.35, and outside took the Rock Channel without difficulty, it being half-tide: Llandudno Bay was reached in two hours. The pier was crowded as the steamer came alongside, the band of the Indefatinuable, on board, playing "God bless the Prince of Wales." Steaming round the Great Ortne, Beaumaria was reached in due course, and a few minutes later Bangor, where the great bulk of those remaining on the vessel disembarked, and spent a couple of hours in visiting the cathedral and various spots of interest in the locality. Captain Owen Lewis found no difficulty in handling the steamer, either in the straits or elsewhere, and at the various sta- tions on the out and home trips the exchange of passengers was effected without delay. All on board expressed delight ar the comfort of the vessel, the spaciousness of her •saloons, and the splendid reach of the promenade deck. With such a steamer on the service an enormous development of the Welsh Coast traffic is confidently anticipatsd. Those who have worked to bring about a better service on this station may be warmly congratulated on the success of their efforts in securing a boat like the St. Tudno, the best of her kind built, and combining high speed with roominess and luxury. Granted careful attention in the catering depart- ment, the greyhound ot the Welsh Coast service is sure of plenty of patronage. The sailings for Whit- week are advertised in our columns.

div.head: COMPENSATION QUESTION.
div.p: THE COMPENSATION QUESTION.

On Tuesday, the tendon County Council, by 60 votes to 38, passed a resolution that the compensation clauses of tho Government Licenses Bill, if passed, would place the Council in a difficult and invidious position, and justify the claim; of the publicans to a vested interest in their licenses. _ _ _

The Congregational Union of Ireland concluded its session on Thursday at Carrickfergus. Resolutions were adopted in favour of Mr. Thomas Lea's bill for securing the permanence of Sunday closing in Ireland and asking the Government to withdraw their licensing proposals, The licensed victuallers of Manchester and Salford at a meeting held on Thursday afternoon adopted a resolution in favour of the Government'slicensing proposals. They also carried a motion condemning as "inconsistent, un- truthful, and highly reprehensible" the conduct of those who are opposing the bill. • Lord Ilarting,ton, replying to a resclution passed by the Rossendale Liberal executive protesting against the crea- tion of a continuous vested interest in :annual liquor licenses, says he should object as strongly as anyone to this, but he fails to see that the grant to public bodies of a sum of Money to be used at their discretion for the purchase and extinction of licenses which have already a recognised market•value can have such an effect. The opposition, he maintained, was hol- low and artificial in its character. an agitation not in favour of tempera...6e, but fostered to injure the Govern- ment. 'MR. GLADSTONE ANT) ENDOWMENT OF PUBLICANS. . _

The following letter from Mr. Gladstone has been re- ceived by the Rev. W. Barker, rector of St. Maryiebone, on the subject of compensation to publicans : " Dear Mr. Barker,—l see, nothing in the resolution herewith returned which requires My interposition, and I think it good that the groat meeting should be truly popular, and should stand apart from party leadership. The money to be laid .out is in itself considerable, vet it is hardly a feather's weight in comparison with the fresh value it would create in all the goodwills on which it does not operate directly. I may bewrong, but it is my firm opinion that the bill will 'at once, and before a single public-house is brought out, add, largely,. sav perhaps 20 per cent., to the value of every public- house in the country. This addition might mean for the three kingdoms £50,000,000 and upwards. Hence it is that I have called it the Public-house Endowment Bill. I do not:question the intention, but the blow to the cause of temperance is the heaviest ever struck.—Yours most faithfully, "Rev. W. Barker, W. E. GLADSTONE. " P.S.—ltou are at liberty to use this letter as you please."

div.head: SHIP CANAL MYSTERY.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL MYSTERY.
CAPTURE OF VAUGHAN.

The unremitting exerdons of the police in their search for the man Vaughan, who disappeared on the day plaman was found shot on the Ship Canal, near Hollinfare, have at Jut been rewarded with success. About nine o'clock yesterday morning, Superintendent Weir,who resides at Leigh, received a telegram from the police at Ross, Herefordshire, where the parents of Vaughan live, announcing that the missing man had been arrested. The tele gram only intimated the fact that the arrest had taken place, bat itis surmised that Vaughan, having reached home, was apprehended during the night by the local police. Immediately upon receiving the telegram, Superintendent Weir left Leigh for Ross,where he will take charge of the prisoner, who will no doubt be charged within the next two or three days with having caused the death of Ma- mma.

div.head: ADJOURNED INQUEST.
div.p: THE ADJOURNED INQUEST.

The adjourned inquest was to be held yesterday,' at Hollinfare, but the Coroner (Mr. S. Brighonse) on arriv- ing at that place was informed of the capture of Vaughan, and at once made arrangements for a further adjournment. Mr. Brighouse informed the jury that when he came there that morning he thought they would be able to finish the inquest. He thought the efforts of the police to find Vaughan had been fruitless, but they would ascertain from Mr. Weir's clerk that Vaughan had been arrested the previous night at Ross, in Hereford- shire, and that Mr. Weir was on his way there to take charge of him. That being so it was only justice to the man not to take any evidence in his absence, but to ad- journ the inquiry until Vaughan was there to bear all that had been said and all that was to be said, so that he might call any evidence he liked or make any statement he liked.

Joseph Rutter, a police 'constable who acts as clerk in Superintendent Weir's office, gave evidence as to the re- ceipt of the telegram, and the departure of Superinten- dent Weir. The telegram was received just before nine o'clock,and Superintendent Weir left at ten minutes past nine. niS instructions were to ask for an adjournment In order that the prisoner might be brought before tha jury. It was then decided to adjourn the inquest till Tuesday, the 3rd of June.

div.head: DISTRICT CONVENTION OF GOOD TEMPLA.RS.
div.p: DISTRICT CONVENTION OF GOOD TEMPLA.RS.
THE CoMPENSATION PROPOSALS.

A convention of the Good Templar lodges in St. Helens, Warrington, Earlestown and district, com- prising the No. I area of South West Lancashire. was held in St. Thomas's Schools, Peter-st., St. Helens, on Saturday afternoon. In the unavoidable absence of Brother Colour-Sergeant Devlin, of War- rington, the Convention Chief Templar, the chair was occupied by Bro. J. Vint, of Ashton-in-Makerfield, Convention Counsellor. There was a good attendance of representatives from St. Helens, Warrington, Earles- town, Golborne, Ashton-in-Makerfield, &c. • Bro. E. Newmann of Earlestown, C.C. Sec., presented his monthly report, which showed the lodges and temples in the area to be doing an active work. The lodge reports showed an increased membership on the whole. A reso- lution was passed that in future the reports of the lodges should be submitted each quarter instead of monthly as hitherto, and a Committee was appointed to visit and assist weak lodges in the district. Altouching reference was made to the loss sustained by the death of Bro. J. E. Pickersgill D.E.S., and it was remarked that his last public appearance was at the last session of the Conven- tion. A vote of condolence with the widow and family was unanimously adopted. It was decided that the next meeting of the Convention should be held at Orford barracks. Warrington. Brother George Pun- shon (St. Helens) afterwards moved "That this meet- ing of Good Templars representing lodges in St. Helens, Warrington, Earlestown, Ashton, Golborne, lc., protests against Government proposals for Providing funds to compensate publicans by which a continuous vested in- terest in annual drink licences is assumed : and this Con- vention respectfully iequests members of Parliament re- presenting borough or county divisions in this area, to vote against any such proposals." Bro. R. Thompson seconded the resolution, which was carried unanimously, and it was decided to send copies to Sir Gilbert Greenall, M.P. for Warrington ; Mr. H. Seton-Karr, M.P. for St. Helens: and Mr. T. W. Legh, M.P. for the Newton Division. A resolution was also passed that therHindley Lodge should be affiliated to the Convention, and Bro. G. R. Allison gave An addmas on "The Arrow"—the district Good Templar periodical. After the session had concluded, about 60 friends partook of an excellent tea, and an open-air meeting followed. In the evening an entertainment was given in the schoolroom, under the presidency of Bro. George Clarke, of' Earlestown. An interesting programme of songs, reckations, &c., was rendered bv Messrs. J. Taylor, Greenough, and Suther- land, and Misses Edwardson, Sutherland, and Bro. Alli- son (Liverpool), gave an appropriate address, and the meeting concluded with votes of thanks.

div.head: MANUFACTURE OE CYCLES IN
div.p: THE MANUFACTURE OE CYCLES IN
WARRINGTON.

About the latest addition to the industries of Warrington, is the manufacture of cycles, which is now being carried on by the Winellie Company, who have set up more extensive premises than might be generally imagined. The company is com- paratively a new one, but, under the management of Mr. Groat, work at the premises is getting brisk. Yesterday an " Examiner" reporter visited the works, and witnessed the process of making the machines, which is one of no little interest. The Wine file tricycle, or " trike," as it is celled in the trade, is one of the most recent productions of the company, and a short trial proved it to be a marvel of strength combined with un- usual lightness. Another machine that emanates from this establishment is an admirable safety hicycl.t, that is fast coming into good repute. The "Liverpool Athletic Times" states the belief that the machines of the Winallie Cycle Company only require to get known to become popular, and goes on to say that, with the object of getting the machines about 1 among local residents, Mr. J. 13. Warren. the St. Helens long-distance rider, has been disporting himself upon a Winallie Safety, out of which he appears' to be getting some pretty good speed. His last perform- I ance was on Sunday, when, in a race of the Sandlield C.C., he started behind scratch, soon after got to the front, and led the whole of the way to the finish. The distance covered was 26 miles; and Warren's time was 1 hour and 40 min. This, too, he could have beaten had it not been that he was pacemaking for a competitor. The race resulted as follows: E. Kerr, Ist, 1 hour 42 min. ;H. Hue,sin, 2nd, 1 hour 50 min. J. Candlish, 3rd, 1 hour 56 min. Kerr, who won this lace:, last year had been training for some little time before the race, and was considered as having a very good chance; of repeating his last year's performance. At the same ! time there were several other members who were consi- tiered to have equally good chances in the race. 'Ale winner was taken in band by Mr. Warren, who was mounted on a Winallie Spring Frame Safety, and S. I Currie, who coached Kerr along at a very nice pace until, they had got him clear of the remaining crowd of coin. I petitors after the first few miles hal been covered- t - ' I After Prescott Hill had been mounted, the o settled down to a very fast pace, and mile after mile' was polished off in splendid time, Kerr still riding well. On reaching the turning point at Sankey Rridges, refreshments were given to the three men laft the secre- tary of the Winallie Cycle Co., and some members qf the Warrington C.C., and at this point P. W. Fair. of the• Warrington C.C., joined in at pacemaking,, the lot start- ing on their return journey at a rattling pace, Kerr still going in splendid form. At Sankey Chapel he was left in charge of Warren and Fair; Currie remaining behind and bringing on seine of the other men. Warren still coached his man in splendid style, and Kerr seemed as fresh at Prescot as when he started, and kept up a splendid pace to the finish, which was reached in]. hour tvid 42 min. Warren finished close upon 200 yards in front, thus doing the fastest time in the race. The diatame covered was ully 26 miles instead of 25, •

div.p: CABINET CONNCIL.

A Cabinet Council was held at the Foreign Office at 11.30 a.m. yesterday, when all. the. Ministers- were pre- sent. The Ministers only sat an hour and lc quarter. The Press Association understands,that no decision was come to on the question of an Autumn, &mkt% there being still nearly three months in, which Emisters can press forward their three principal,ffills.

div.p: STANLEY V: TROUP..

In Mr. instice North's Court yesterday motion to restrain the defendant in the action of Stanley v. Troup from publishing an account of the march of the Rear Column of Ernin.Pasha'i relief expedition wassannounc- ed to have been settled by agreement, by whicisthe pro- ceedings will be stayed and the defendant be allbwed to publish his book on the 15th October' next. Ms. Justice North concurred. THE MURDER OF A BARMAID..

An inquest was held yesterday„. in London, on the body of Florence Varney, .publican's daughter, who was shot on Wednesday, at Kentish TOWII{ by Thos. Harding. The mother of the deceased said Harding asked deceased to go out with him,.but she refused. He said no one else should have her, and shot her.. Dr. Beaton said death was caused by bullet wounds in the neck mu jaw, and the jury, after a short deliberation fonnd a verdict of wilful murder against Harding.

div.head: GATHERING OF, PRIMITIVE METHODISTS.
div.p: GATHERING OF, PRIMITIVE METHODISTS.

On Saturday the fraternal association of officials and members of the Preston Brook, Lymm, St. Helens, Warrington, Widnes, Barlestown, and Low- ton circuits met at the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Lymm. There was a very. good gathering, Widnes furnishing a, large contingent. Among those .present were—The Revs. A. tpa Morn,. Stockport ; J. Dudley, Lowton ; W. aham; Warrington; C. Finch, Runcorn ;.and W. Evans,,Lyram ; Messrs. S. Owens, T. Rolleson. S. Drought, T. Pinches, and C. Sage, from Simms Cross ; J Bissell and A. Graham, War- rington ;;lE. Bancroft. Beinhan3 ; G. L. Welford and Warburton, Lymm ; Ji T.. Ambler, Timperley.• The afternoon session was presided over by the Rev. W. Evans;.when a very admirable paper on "Family Religion" was read by-BiPr... X.. T. Ambler, the discussion upon it being opened by the Rev. C. Finch, the Revs. Dudley and J. A. Mortor4.and Messrs. Bancroft, Warbur- ton, and Sage taking. past. On the motion of the Rev. C. Finch,, seconded by. the Rev. W. Graham a hearty vote of thanks. was accorded Mr. Ambler for his instruc- tive paper. Tea was.subsequedtly partaken of in the schoolroom, after which the friends interested them- selves by rambling around the village and admiring its lovely scenery. The evening meeling was presided over by Mr. G. L.-Welford-,, when addresses were delivered on the following subjects', " The mission of atrue church," by Mr. S. Owens ;: '" The =motives to action of a true church,"' by. the Rev. C. Finch; and "The characteris- tics of a true church," by the Rev. A. Morten. The meeting' was of- a.uioAt interesting and profitable charac- ter'. The usual votes of thanks were passed; and the visitors exzwessedi their warm thanks to the Melbas at Lyinm for the very efficient provision made for their en- jeyment, anaat the very satisfactory way in whigh all the arrangements had been carried out.

CLERK OF THE PEACE'S OFFICE, PRESTON 19TH MAY, 1890. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that a General SESSION of the Peace for the County Palatine of Lancaster will be holden at the COUNTY SESSIONS HOUSE, ISLINGTON, IN LIVERPOOL, ON TUESDAY THE TENTH DAY OF JUNE next, at eleven o'clock in the forenoon precisely. The Solicitors engaged in prosecutions at the said Session are requested to take notice that all instructions for indict- ments and depositions are required to be sent to the Clerk of the Peace's Office seven days at least before the said Session. F. C. HULTON. Clerk of the Peace.
